5.label: Top: a premature knight sortie (almost all f3g5/Ng5, plus Nb5/Nb4) drops the undefended knight to a trivial queen grab (Qxg5) or queen check (Qa5+/Qa4+); medium blurs to other knight moves (Nh4, Ng4, Na5) and even bishop/queen moves that hang material or merely lose tempo rather than hanging outright.

6.label: Top: a knight greedily grabs the d4/d5 central pawn and is immediately recaptured (usually by Qxd4), dropping a piece for a pawn; medium broadens to any piece (bishop/queen) capturing on central squares (e5 as well as d4) that gets recaptured, plus a few non-capture hangs.

12.label: At the peak the player surrenders the active (usually dark-squared) bishop with a check-capture on c3/d2 (Bxc3+/Bxd2+), releasing a pin/central tension and forgoing a stronger tactical continuation (Qxd4, Nxe4); at medium it broadens to other check-captures (Bxc6+/Bxd7+) that likewise trade off the strongest, pressure-generating piece prematurely—materially a safe trade but forfeiting the advantage.

9.label: Top fires on materially-safe endgame moves that throw away a clearly winning position (underpromotion, trading into insufficient material, walking into a fork); medium blurs to opening tempo/positional errors (Ke7) that concede the advantage without losing material — plus several near-0cp false positives.

13.label: Top boards consistently hang a piece/exchange/queen to a clean, immediate capture by ignoring an existing attacker or capturing into a trap (hanging_piece); medium boards blur this into slower or non-clean losses—tempo losses, endgame king/pawn races, structural concessions, and missed wins of trapped pieces—where the material damage unfolds over several moves rather than in one ply.

11.label: Top boards walk the king (or a guarding piece) into a forced, often smothered, mate by ignoring an obvious saving capture; medium broadens to the same tactical oversight that merely drops a piece/pawn or squanders the win rather than getting mated.

2.label: Top: a quiet/natural move skips a winning knight-check fork on the exposed/uncastled king (typically Nd6+ or Nd3+ winning the queen/piece); medium broadens to any missed forcing king tactic — other knight checks (Ng4+, Nc2+, Nb4+, Nxf6+), zwischenzug move-orders, or queen checks/perpetuals.

18.label: Top: king walks to an exposed square (Kd2/Kf2) and gets hit by a winning rook check on the 2nd-rank/e-file (one case a knight fork); medium blurs into king-centralization moves (Kf5/Kg7) that are actually engine-best in lost positions, so it flags king-into-check geometry whether or not it's a real blunder.

4.label: Top: a rook (or king) deserts its defensive post—dropping a pawn or walking into a rook-mating net (king-safety motifs)—while medium broadens to any undefended piece (bishop/knight/rook) left en prise, or a lost tempo in a promotion race, via fork/skewer/back-rank shots.

1.label: Top: in a 100%-winning position the player greedily grabs a seemingly-free piece/queen, neglecting an in-between move/recapture or leaving its own piece hanging so the 'free' material is recovered with interest; medium broadens the refutation type to captures that walk into forks and discovered checks (plus one quiet move that misses a forced mate).

16.label: Top: a move (often castling or a capture) vacates a piece's/square's only defender and is punished by a forced recapture into a knight fork or decisive capture; medium keeps the removed-defender hang but blurs into tempo-losing retreats, greedy captures, and other tactical oversights — and a minority of boards are instead missed winning captures.

15.label: Top: a bishop is developed straight onto an undefended square and captured for free (Ba6/Bg5/Bg4/Ba3); medium keeps the hung bishop but blurs to an indirect loss (Bb5 met by Bxb5+) and a non-hang outlier (missed Nd6+ fork).

21.label: Top: from a winning position White/Black recaptures with the wrong piece (queen/king instead of knight), leaving a now-undefended knight to a simple pawn break like ...exd4/dxe5; medium broadens to any move that drops a minor piece in a better position—pawn captures (fxe5, gxh3), forks (Nxf7+, Qe4), or trapped bishops—rather than only mis-recaptures.

8.label: Top boards are constant: in a near-lost position the player makes a capture/recapture (usually rook or queen) that strips away the last defending piece, yielding either a back-rank mate or a decisive queen/rook trade that kills all counterplay; medium blurs this into broader defensive lapses—non-capturing king-safety blunders, ignored mate threats, hung minors, or premature trades when behind—that all hasten the loss.

0.label: Top boards are Italian/Two-Knights structures with a tactically-supported knight (usually White's Nd5 behind a Bg5/Bh4 pin) where a quiet or wrong-order move instead of the forcing Nxe7+ hangs the knight/bishop to ...Nxd5; medium broadens to any abandoned forcing knight capture-with-check (Nxf3+, Nxd3+, Nxe3+, Nxf6+) so the dropped piece/missed win is more varied and occasionally a missed win/mate rather than a hung piece.

23.label: Top: in the opening Black retreats the attacked f7-king (to e8/g6/e7) instead of the only move Qxg5, leaving the g4-bishop hanging to the uniform refutation Qxg4 (which also re-defends the g5-knight); medium keeps the king-flight-that-drops-material theme but blurs to other squares and pieces — e.g. Kf2-f1/Kh2-g1 dropping a bishop, or Kb7-a7 hanging a rook and walking into mate.

27.label: In a won opening the player skips an immediate free capture, playing a natural developing/pawn move instead; at the top the hanging victim is always a bishop (e.g. dxc4, Qxg4), while medium broadens to any undefended piece left en prise—bishop, but also knight (Qxh5, Bxb5) or queen (gxh5).

20.label: Top: a routine developing/castling move (O-O, Nf3, h3, Ne2, dxe6) ignores a forcing queen check or capture (Qa4+, Qxg4, Bxf7+) that wins a loose bishop on b4/g4 against an uncastled king; medium keeps the same 'winning position → played safe move → missed exploiting a loose piece' idea but broadens the target to the b4-knight and other tactics (Qd5, ...e5/...d3), with a few cases that actually hang material or are positional rather than pure missed wins.

42.label: Top: a winning rook (or major piece) endgame thrown away by leaving the rook en prise to the adjacent enemy KING; medium keeps the hung-rook-in-endgame theme but broadens the capturer to any piece (bishop/rook/queen) or a simple tactic (fork, back-rank, zwischenzug).

10.label: At the peak it's a rook misplayed—captured greedily or relocated passively—that drops material or forgoes a winning active-rook plan (7th-rank/doubling); at medium the same forfeit-the-material-edge error blurs across knights, bishops, pawns and wrong-piece placements, and mixes hanging own material with missing a win.

43.label: Top is the unsound Nxf7 knight sacrifice (Fried Liver-style, no supporting development) where the king/rook just recaptures; medium broadens to any over-optimistic knight jump-in (Nxf2, Nc7+, Nf3+, Nxc2, Nxe6) that's simply taken, all hanging the knight for a pawn or nothing.

44.label: Top boards are rook checks in drawn/losing endgames that squander the critical defensive/winning tempo by driving the enemy king to a superior square; medium blurs to other pieces (queen checks) and even includes harmless or optimal checks (false positives).

32.label: Top boards consistently drop material because a forced pawn recapture is pinned/illegal—opening a file that wins the queen (or king); medium broadens to displaced or overloaded queens that fail their defensive role and lose material to a break.

50.label: At the peak the player makes a quiet non-capturing move (often the SEE-flagged knight move) in a drawn endgame that leaves the queen undefended/under attack and loses it outright; at medium the pattern blurs to hanging other material (minor piece, rook), allowing mate, and even includes near-equal non-blunders, so the unifying thread is only 'own material lost on a non-capturing move.'

19.label: Top boards squander a forced mate (mostly mate-in-1/2) by playing a tempting but inferior forcing move — wrong move-order, wrong piece, or wrong check — instead of the precise mating/winning blow; the medium board shows the identical pattern (Qa1+ thrown in for the mating Qxh2+), though a minority actively hang material in the refutation rather than merely skip the win.

55.label: At the peak, an already-winning side plays a quiet or wrong-piece move that throws away an immediate forced mate (often mate-in-1/2, e.g. Bxd8 instead of Qxd8#); at medium it broadens to missing longer forced mates (mate-in-3/4) or forcing tactical check-sequences from a won position.

36.label: Top boards are all flashy QUEEN checks (Qc8+/Qd8+/Qa8+) tossed in instead of a free capture or forced mate—the king walks and the queen is left offside; medium blurs to any premature check, adding ROOK checks (Re1+/Rd1+) and cases that merely squander a winning advantage or tempo rather than a clean mate/piece.

29.label: Top boards are gambit openings where the player's d-pawn could win the loose Nc3 with dxc3 but instead a routine developing/pawn move (d5, Nf6, f5, f6, Bc5) leaves the central pawn hanging to recapture; medium broadens to general opening central-pawn-tension errors that drop or mis-capture a central pawn (exd5/cxd5/dxe4 motifs) rather than the specific knight-grab.

54.label: Top boards constantly miss Qxd5 to trade off the dominant centralized enemy queen (often hanging material to it instead); medium broadens to other neglected neutralizing queen exchanges (c6/d3/e6) and a couple of missed attacking shots.

60.label: Top: hangs the queen outright by skipping a forcing queen-trade (Qxe2+) on an open e-file; medium broadens to losing other material (e.g. a trapped knight) or just forfeiting advantage by declining the analogous forcing exchange/check.

33.label: Top: a quiet king/defensive move from an already-lost position drops a whole piece/queen or the game outright, frequently because the refutation's capture, recapture, or promotion comes WITH CHECK (Rxc4+, Rxe7+, e8=Q+, Rxg3+); medium blurs to dropping just a pawn or conceding a positional/king-safety edge via similar exposing moves, with the decisive 'fatal check' detail no longer constant.

56.label: Top: while already winning, the player skips a crushing queen capture/incursion against an exposed king (Qxh6, Qh3, Qxa7) and instead plays a slow pawn/developing move; medium blurs to missing winning blows by any piece (Bxd6, Rxa7, a4) or allowing a trade/quiet check that dissolves the advantage.

52.label: Top: a queen move permits a forced queen trade that dissolves a winning attack or loses material in the simplification; medium broadens to any queen/minor-piece move that abandons a key defensive duty, conceding material or a counterattack rather than specifically a queen swap.

57.label: Top: a forcing queen trade (capture, almost always with check) simplifies into a king-and-pawn endgame that throws away the win or draw; medium keeps the same 'eliminate the strong piece by a forcing simplification' error but broadens the traded material to rook trades, queen-for-rook sacs, and promotions whose new queen is immediately recaptured (plus rarer non-trade simplifications).

62.label: Top: skips the winning queen pawn-grab (almost always Qxg2, sometimes Qxb7) that punishes an uncastled central king, playing a quiet move that lets the opponent castle/consolidate; medium broadens to missing any decisive winning continuation — hanging-piece captures (Qxh7), tactical double-threats, or forced mates — and bleeds into a few outright hangs.

64.label: Top: a premature central/flank pawn advance (d5, g5, b5, c5, e5) directly drops a pawn or piece to a simple capture or king attack; medium broadens to pawn pushes (b4, e4, g4) that enable a knight fork or a premature release of central tension that wins material.

45.label: Top boards drop the queen to a forcing capture/discovered-check or walk the king into an immediate (often back-rank) mate; medium broadens to ignoring a tactic that hangs a minor piece or pawn, or merely surrenders the win to a draw/perpetual.

69.label: Top: a natural developing/castling move in an equal opening leaves a centralized knight (overwhelmingly e5, also e4/d5) undefended while attacked, dropping a full piece to an immediate free capture; medium blurs the target to any piece, the exchange, or even simply missed wins, with material lost through deeper multi-move tactics (forks, deflections, opened diagonals) and extending into endgames.

66.label: Top boards consistently hang the c6/c3 knight to a diagonal capture-with-check (Bxc6+ / Nxc3 then Bxc3+) that wins the exchange or a piece in the opening; medium boards keep the 'undefended minor piece in the opening' core but blur the motif to any hung/forked knight or bishop (Qxc3+, Qxg4, Qa4+) and even a few near-positional drops.

70.label: Top: a winning side plays a quiet/pawn move that fails to grab a free, undefended enemy KNIGHT (which then escapes via a trade); medium broadens to missing other hanging pieces (e.g. a bishop) and more generally to squandering a won position—including letting one's own material drop over the next move or two.

68.label: Top boards are premature queen trades (frequently Qxd1) that walk into a zwischenzug/fork or relinquish a winning attack; medium blurs into bishop/minor-piece captures that surrender a key defender or quietly drop material.

73.label: Top boards hang a corner rook (h1/a1/h8) to an infiltrated enemy queen after a careless developing/central move; medium broadens to hanging any piece (bishop, knight, pawn) captured by a queen or knight.

78.label: Top boards are all a greedy bishop grabbing a defended pawn (overwhelmingly Bxc7) that the enemy queen recaptures for free, losing a full piece; medium keeps the hung bishop but blurs it to non-capturing developments (Bg4) and multi-move refutations (Bxe2 opening lines), plus one queen-move missed-win outlier.

59.label: Top: a won pawn/piece endgame is thrown away by failing to directly capture or eliminate the opponent's lone dangerous passed pawn (Nxa6, Nxa4, Kxh4, Nxh4+, Qxg6+), usually choosing a tempo-wasting check or wrong-target capture instead; medium blurs to broader passed-pawn-race technique failures — missed deflection checks (d3+), wrong king routing (Kf7/Kd5), or premature pawn pushes — plus a few that slide into actually hanging/trading the piece.

85.label: Top boards are uniformly routine developing/castling moves that pass up a winning Greek Gift sacrifice (Bxh7+/Bxh2+) in already-winning openings; medium blurs to any squandered tactical shot in winning positions (forks, central breakthroughs, exchange-winning captures, perpetual-check) plus a few moves that outright hang material.

90.label: Top positions are quiet 'activating/repositioning' moves (Rg3, Qf3, Rad1, Na5) that ignore the opponent's threat and walk into a concrete material-winning refutation — pin, fork, or passed-pawn breakthrough; medium broadens to positional moves (c3) that concede ~300cp by letting the opponent's plan proceed unchallenged without an immediate material tactic.

24.label: At the peak: a king move (or pawn/rook collapse) in an already-lost endgame that walks into or accelerates forced mate; at medium it blurs into any piece's move that merely worsens a difficult/losing position without an actual forced mate.

63.label: Top boards: a misguided king/queen/pawn repositioning move that ignores a concrete threat loses material to a forcing tempo-tactic (fork, queen-attack, trap, hanging piece); medium boards: the same neglect broadens into king-safety collapses—mating attacks, back-rank and discovered checks.

96.label: At the peak the player has a forced mate (mate-in-1/2, almost all back-rank/king-safety) and throws it away with a tempting capture or rook-doubling on the 2nd rank; at medium it blurs into squandering any winning advantage—missing decisive material wins or attacking lines, hanging a piece, or a positional/tempo collapse—plus a couple of false positives where the flagged move was actually best.

72.chip: Missed precise endgame conversion (often forced win)
72.label: Top boards throw away a fully decided endgame (won or drawn) via a natural king move, free-pawn capture, or wrong promotion that skips the one precise resource — frequently a forced mate or material-winning tactic; medium broadens to milder conversion slips that stay winning (tempo loss, lesser underpromotion, sometimes not even blunders).

83.label: Top fires on a king move—usually an automatic Kxpawn—that loses or fails to win a pure king-and-pawn endgame (several are 0cp 'errors' in already-lost positions); medium broadens to any greedy capture or careless king/pawn move that hangs material or misses the win in late positions.

80.chip: King steps into checks (mate or material)
80.label: Top: a king retreat drops the king into a perpetual-check or mating net, squandering a forced win; medium: the king goes to a slightly worse square (single-square errors) where the opponent's checks instead win material or escape to a draw.

91.label: At the peak the player gives a tempo-gaining rook check (or otherwise temporizes) instead of queening immediately in a won R+P/K+P endgame; at medium this broadens to pawn pushes and king shuffles that likewise skip the cleanest, fastest promotion—material stays safe and the position usually remains winning, so it reads as a missed cleanest conversion rather than a blunder.

97.label: Top: in a completely won endgame the king sidesteps (Ke7/Kh3/Ke2/Kf5 etc.) instead of grabbing a free undefended rook—occasionally a queen or pawn—throwing away the win; medium blurs from 'capture the hanging rook' to 'find the one decisive resource,' adding missed promotion technique, pure tempo losses, and even hanging a piece to a queen fork.

95.label: Top: a queen/king move (often declining the saving Qxqueen trade) leaves the king exposed to a forcing checking/mating sequence (Rg1+, Qf2#, Qg8+, f1=Q#); medium: blurs from king-hunts to any passive queen reposition or pawn move that simply drops material or squanders the advantage (Qa5, Qe4, Re3, Nxf2).

88.label: Top: an aggressive rook lunge to the enemy/own back rank (d8, e8, c8, b8, g1, d1) hangs the rook (or loses heavy material) to a forced recapture/deflection/discovery sequence; medium broadens to any rook move — plus occasional king/pawn/knight moves — that either hangs a piece or accepts a losing trade/tactic that simplifies into a lost endgame.

107.label: Top: a quiet move leaves an undefended piece (often Bg5) for the enemy QUEEN to snap off along an open line; medium broadens the capturer to rooks/bishops (and victim to knights) and adds king moves that walk into a free capture.

110.label: Top is a queen grabbing the central d4 pawn (Qxd4) in a level opening, punished by Qxb7/Bb5+ that wins the a8-rook or the queen; medium broadens to other greedy queen sorties/pawn-grabs (Qxd5, Qxb7, Qg3) refuted with tempo and net material loss — though a few odd boards (Bc5 missed win, ...e6, Rxd2) blur the theme.

84.label: Top: consistently a greedy capture (grabbing a pawn/piece) that hangs material to a recapture, infiltration, or fork—often exploiting the player's own exposed king; medium: blurs to any active/misplaced or even passive move that overlooks the critical tactical demand, including cases where a materially-safe move skips a winning capture/mate.

103.label: Top boards constantly move the queen (or recapture with king) onto a square allowing a check-first knight fork that wins the queen; medium boards keep the knight-fork theme but blur the target to rook/exchange (Nc2+, Nd3+, Nd7+) and add a few non-fork piece-trapping tactics.

105.label: Top: a move exposes the king or removes a guard, refuted by a forcing (usually queen) check that wins a piece/exchange or mates; medium blurs the refutation away from checks toward any loose-material grab — plain captures of undefended pieces/pawns and non-check forks.

113.label: Top boards are almost uniformly hanging the f6 knight to White's e5 pawn (ignoring exf6 with moves like h6/Be7/Qe7/d3/dxc3), while medium broadens to mishandling that same attacked knight with structural/positional cost (exf6 gxf6 doubled pawns, trading the advanced d5 pawn, or losing material to a follow-up fork) rather than a clean piece drop.

114.label: Top: a minor piece (usually a knight ...Nxe4, also bishop Bxd5/Bxb4) greedily snatches an 'apparently free' opening pawn and loses material—either the capturer is hung to an intermezzo check (Qa4+/Bb4+) or it abandons a key defender (g7/f7); medium keeps the greedy-grab core but blurs to queen pawn-snatches that get trapped (Qxb2, Bxa7→Rxe2+) and other tactic-ignoring or tempo-wasting moves (Bg4, b4, Ng5).

99.label: At the peak an aggressive piece move or check drops a whole piece (often to a pawn) and throws away a forced mate; at medium it broadens to hanging only a pawn, allowing a slower mate, or a quiet/inaccurate move that merely squanders the won position rather than cleanly hanging material.

121.label: Top: voluntarily exchanges queens (Qx capture) into a clearly lost king-and-pawn endgame, throwing away a draw/win whose only resource was keeping queens on; medium broadens the same 'simplify into a lost ending' error to rook trades (Rx into lost pawn endings) and a few wrong-order captures, with the constant being a needless trade that converts an equal/better position into a losing simplified endgame.

120.label: Top: in a winning position the player makes a slow/wrong-order move and misses a forcing intermediate bishop check (deflection/clearance sacrifice) that wins material; medium broadens to other missed winning tactics—forks, knight checks, zwischenzugs—plus a couple of cases that outright hang the queen.

118.label: Top boards hang the queen—usually a flashy 'free' check like Qh5+ that walks straight into the enemy queen on the open 5th rank; medium broadens to hanging any piece or, more loosely, abandoning a key defender so the king's safety collapses into a forced mate.

112.label: Top boards almost all relocate or greedily trade a strong, centralized knight off its key (defensive/controlling) square and lose material to the tactical refutation; medium blurs to other pieces (bishops) and even pawn pushes that abandon a defender or walk into a fork/capture, occasionally just missing a forcing win.

116.label: At the peak, a pawn push/promotion (e.g. b8=Q, ...h2, Qd6+) hangs material and throws away a clearly won endgame; at medium activation the pattern blurs into missing a winning tactic (Rxf3+ fork) or losing tempo, i.e. any failure to convert a winning position rather than a strict material hang.

128.label: Top boards centralize a piece (esp. bishop to d5) straight into a trap or abandon its defended knight, losing material at once; medium broadens to queen/rook redeployments that vacate a key file or shield, conceding material/king safety over the next 2-3 moves.

129.label: Top: from a winning position the player skips a forcing knight leap/fork (Nxc6, Ne6, Nc6, Ne3) that hits the queen plus a second piece—often with a check (Nxe7+/Nxg7+)—to win material, instead playing a quiet/prophylactic move; medium: same missed-win-via-passive-move pattern, but the unfound shot broadens from knight forks to other winning tactical captures (Bxh3, Bxb2, Bxc3, Bxe6, Qxg5) and occasional non-knight motifs.

115.label: Top: drawn rook/pawn endgames where the player pushes their own pawn or makes a pointless check/king move instead of capturing or blockading the opponent's passed pawn, converting a draw into a loss; medium broadens to any failure to meet the critical threat — still often a passer, but also ignored mates, missed blockades, and a few missed winning conversions.

98.label: At the peak the player, while completely winning, ignores a free hanging rook (sometimes losing their own piece in the mutual-capture race); at medium the same skipped free capture broadens to undefended queens and a knight.

127.label: Top: in an already-won endgame the player makes a greedy small pawn-grab or quiet move that skips the decisive capture—often an undefended rook (Kxe6/Rxd8)—throwing the win away; medium broadens to tempo-losing, move-order king moves (Kc5/Kf1/Kc1) that surrender the win or draw without any capture, plus some false positives where the flagged move was actually best.

122.label: Top: in a clearly winning opening, a 'natural' quiet/retreating/developing move passes up a forcing winning capture (very often Nxg5, plus Nxc7+/Nxc6/b4); medium keeps the same quiet-move-ignores-tactics root but blurs in direction — now the calm move frequently also hangs own material to a fork or capture rather than merely skipping a win.

108.label: Top: a passive queen retreat/reposition skips the only winning capture (repeatedly Bxf3 exploiting an f3-knight pin), squandering a won game; medium keeps the passive-queen DNA but blurs to other missed tactics (forks, back-rank, forced mates) and other quiet king/piece moves that even walk into mate or hang material.

125.label: Top: in a completely won endgame, played a quiet pawn/king move instead of grabbing a hanging enemy piece (mostly rooks/queens, sometimes via a mutual capture-race that drops own material); medium broadens to any squandered winning resource — forks, tempo, move-order, or faster mate.

132.label: Top boards miss a clean forcing CAPTURE in a won endgame (repeatedly Rxh3+ winning an undefended knight, also Qxc8+/Qxg6) by playing a quiet or greedy pawn-grab instead—sometimes even hanging their own queen/rook; medium broadens to missing the fastest FORCED MATE or single winning check (Re7+, Rb8+, Qf5+, Rxd4+), and includes several false positives where the played move is actually optimal.

136.label: Top: Scholar's-Mate-style Qxf7+/Qxf2+ capture-check that simply hangs the queen for a pawn to a recapture (Kxf7/Nxf7/Bxf7+); medium broadens to any aggressive queen check/capture elsewhere lost to recapture, intermezzo, or counter-check, plus a few queen trades that throw away a winning attack.

137.label: Top: a backfiring QUEEN check (the 'patzer sees a check' that pointlessly improves White's king or self-hangs the queen to a fork/capture/forced losing trade); medium broadens to checks by rook/knight (and harmful trades), with the consequence blurring between hanging material and squandering a win.

140.label: Top boards uniformly hang the QUEEN to a KNIGHT capture (queen steps onto a knight-controlled square, e.g. Qe3/Qd2 →Nxe3/Nxd2); medium keeps the 'walked own material into a free capture' core but blurs the hung piece (also knight/rook) and the capturer (also pawn/bishop), with a couple of positional/trade material losses mixed in.

134.label: Top: king moves in deeply lost king-and-pawn endgames that fail the only opposition/tempo defense (frequently 0cp 'maximal-resistance' moves); medium broadens to rook endgames and wrong/greedy captures that squander an actual draw or win.

141.label: Top boards uniformly hang a ROOK by moving/leaving it on a square controlled by an enemy BISHOP's diagonal (captured free); medium keeps the rook-onto-bishop's-diagonal motif but broadens the victim to the queen and the capturer to rook (same-rank) or knight, with a couple of positional/tempo slips that merely expose the hanging piece.

124.label: Top: a quiet/loosening pawn advance—usually to chase a bishop (f4 vs Be3, c3 vs Bd4, b3 vs Ba4, g5 vs Bf4)—throws away a winning position, either hanging material (f4, b3, f6-fork) or skipping a forcing capture (dxe5, Nxd4); medium broadens to other tension-releasing pawn moves/captures (b5 allowing e5, exd6) with the same roughly 50/50 hangs-or-misses split.

148.label: At the peak every board is a forced back-rank checkmate (#-1/#-2) on a luft-less h1 king after White removes the back-rank defender (Bxd5, Rxc4) or skips the saving luft push (h3); medium repeats the same defender-removal Rxc4 motif, so the pattern stays tightly back-rank-mate focused with only the trigger (no-luft vs. removed guard) blurring.

135.label: Top boards are sharp greedy captures or king-exposing recaptures (Qxg2+, Rxf5, hxg4, Kxg1, Qc5+) that hang material and bare the player's own king; medium boards blur into slower coordination-losing or tempo-wasting moves (Bh6, b5, Bf2, Qb8+, Nf6) that surrender the attacking initiative and merely squander a won/equal position.

143.label: Top: a rook check (chosen over a forced mate or decisive quiet/pawn move) relocates the enemy king to a better square and squanders the win — geometry constant as 'tempting rook check that lets the king escape the net'; medium broadens to queen/pawn checks and even non-check king/rook repositionings that likewise throw away a mate or a winning advantage (with some bleeding into hung/positional cases).

145.chip: King strays from pawn race (out of square)
145.label: Top: in pure pawn endgames the king marches the wrong way and lands outside the 'square' of the enemy passed pawn, losing the promotion race; medium blurs into broader king-march tempo losses (and even slow pawn pushes) in king-and-pawn / passed-pawn races.

156.label: Top fires on non-forcing/prophylactic 'slow' moves (h4, a3, and even Rfd1/Rg2) that waste a tempo or skip a precise active continuation and let the position slip—ranging from harmless-in-a-lost-game to a tactical refutation; medium narrows to the canonical luft pawn-push (a3) that squanders a winning position into equality.

144.label: Top boards uniformly ignore a free, immediately-capturable enemy QUEEN — the player instead pushes a quiet pawn or develops a knight (often a 'tempo' move that just lets the queen retreat, occasionally even costing the attacking rook); medium broadens to missing other hanging pieces (e.g. a knight via exf4/cxd5) and a winning discovered check, so the constant 'free queen for the taking' loosens to 'free material left on the board.'

150.label: At the peak it's a greedy capture (frequently a knight, often grabbed by the queen) that walks straight into a forced checkmate while ignoring the lethal threat; at medium it blurs to quiet/non-capturing moves (king tucks, rook lifts, retreats) that overlook the opponent's decisive reply and lose material or get forked rather than always being mated.

133.label: At peak activation a piece (often knight or queen) is relocated off a critical square, allowing a decisive check or mate; at medium activation this broadens to other pieces and blurs into ignored winning captures and slower positional/tempo retreats.

159.label: Top: in a winning/attacking position the player picks a passive or non-forcing move and skips an immediate forcing check — almost always a rook (or queen) check on an open file/back rank against an exposed king — that mates or wins material; medium broadens to other missed winning shots where the decisive move is a different forcing resource (pawn-push check, pin-check, capture-with-check, or even a quiet best move like e6/Bd5) and the stakes shrink from forced mate to merely squandering a clear advantage.

130.label: Top: a bishop captures the centralized knight on d4/d5 and the enemy queen recaptures dominantly (Bxd4→Qxd4); medium broadens to rook/pawn/queen-grab captures with varied recapturing pieces, ranging from clean material loss to even-but-lost positional trades.

167.label: Top: a won pawn endgame where the player dawdles with a king move (Kf1/Ke1/Kc7/Kb8) instead of queening the passed pawn at once, letting the opponent promote/perpetual and squander the win or draw; medium broadens to other passed-pawn endgame slips (pawn pushes, rook/queen moves) that mistime conversion, plus a few near-0cp false positives.

171.chip: Hangs queen on a check (any recapture)
171.label: Top: a queen move delivers check but lands en prise and is simply captured by an enemy rook or queen on the checking square (the check is meaningless); medium keeps the queen-check-hangs core but broadens the recapturing piece to knights/pawns that capture while blocking the check, and includes checks that also throw away a forced mate.

153.label: Top: a developing/pawn move ignores a centralized enemy knight (usually Nd5), conceding a knight fork (Nxc7+/Nxe7+) or free capture; medium broadens to line-opening pawn breaks (f6, a6, e5) and defender-removing moves that drop material to varied opening tactics.

157.label: Top: from a winning position the player declines a free capture of a hanging enemy piece (Bxg4/Bxd5/fxe4) and instead makes a quiet developing/pushing move, hanging material to a follow-up tactic; medium broadens to any quiet developing, castling, or repositioning move in a roughly level position that skips a needed capture/exchange and gets punished by a fork, pin, remove-the-guard, or pawn break.

180.label: Top: a rook (sometimes queen) left en prise—often via a losing capture or rook-for-minor trade—throwing away a winning endgame; medium keeps the hung-piece core but blurs to queens lost to skewers/back-rank alignment, trapped/undefended bishops, plus several missed wins and a couple non-blunders.

170.label: Top boards hang a queenside bishop (Ba4/Ba5/Bb4, also Bg5) by maintaining the c3/c6 knight-pin instead of resolving it with the forcing Bxc3+/Bxc6+, so the bishop gets trapped, chased by ...b5/...b4, or forked (Qa4+); medium boards blur to any quiet opening/early-middlegame move that overlooks a forcing tactic (fork, pin, or decisive capture), more often missing a win than actually losing material.

187.label: Top: a knight greedily captures a central pawn (repeatedly Nc6xd4) and is simply recaptured, losing the piece for a pawn; medium blurs to any knight sortie—outpost/check/relocation onto a defended or undefended square (Ne5, Nf5, Nf6, Ne7+, Nxh6+)—that hangs the knight, with a few boards instead being a knight move that skips an immediate material win.

169.label: Top: greedy queen captures forgo an available perpetual or mating check (often exposing own king to mate); medium keeps the missed forcing check but broadens to quiet pawn/king pushes, move-order slips, and non-queen pieces.

188.label: Top: a reflexive capture (often of the queen, sometimes a rook) that throws away an immediate mate-in-one while staying materially winning; medium broadens to move-order slips, premature queen trades, and non-forcing moves that squander a longer forced mate or a winning tactic.

185.label: Top: quiet KING moves in pure king-and-pawn endgames that bungle the promotion race — abandoning a won race (Kf3 not Kxh4, Kg5 not Kg4) or walking the king into the opponent's queening/mating net; medium blurs into knight/rook/bishop and pawn moves that similarly misjudge passed-pawn races and king activity, mixing thrown-away wins with accelerated losses.

183.label: From an already-lost position the player makes a move that throws away more — at the peak it's a sharp sacrifice/hang of a key DEFENSIVE piece (Nxe3, Bxf2+, Rxd1, Bxh2+, Rxg2+) or king-pawn weakening (g3/g4) that exposes the king to forced mate; at medium it blurs to softer king-safety lapses — king walks (Ke2, Kg2), ignored mate threats (Ra8 vs Qe6#), back-rank/tempo errors (Rf6, Ng1, h5, Rfa1) — that still drop material or allow mate over the refutation.

172.label: Top: in a won endgame the player advances a passed pawn (or fires a check) instead of capturing the lone hanging piece/rook, converting the win to a draw/loss; medium keeps the 'tempting move over the only winning move' core but broadens both sides — the played move blurs to any natural choice (premature push, slow developing move, spite check) and the missed win blurs from a capture to any precise resource (king march, correct promotion timing, forced mate or tactic).

191.label: Top boards are opening pawn-kicks of an enemy knight (b5/e5/g5) that ignore a refuting tactic—f6/d6/h6 walking into Qh5+ king attacks, c6/a6/c3 inviting an Nc7+/Nc2+ fork; medium broadens to any tempo-gaining attack on a knight (g4/e4/b4/g5), including piece moves, punished by a wider range of tactics (sacrifices on f2/f7, exchange-winning forks, hanging-piece captures) that all lose material.

175.label: At the peak, a tempo-losing/self-weakening move forfeits a clear or defensible advantage and is refuted by a concrete pawn break or check; at medium it blurs to king-safety pawn moves (e.g. ...g6) that invite a check or fork winning material.

182.chip: Hangs piece, refuted forcing move (often knight check)
182.label: At the peak it's a tempting forcing check—usually a knight fork/sac—whose checking piece is simply captured (or a forced mate squandered), losing material; at medium it blurs to any premature or unsound tactic, often not even a check (bad captures, piece sacs, missed cleaner wins), undone by an overlooked refutation/recapture.

200.label: Top boards are premature pawn advances in king-and-pawn endgames that wreck the structure or allow losing liquidation; medium blurs to any over-committal, tempo-wasting move (rook/king/knight) that worsens an already-difficult endgame, with several near-zero-cp 'non-blunders' diluting the signal.

193.label: Top: in a clearly winning position the player makes a passive queen move and overlooks a clean forcing knockout (usually a knight fork or check winning material/mate); medium broadens the overlooked finish to other pieces and slower forced mates, and some 'errors' are only marginally suboptimal.

199.label: Top is uniformly missed mate-in-one via a queen capture against a boxed-in king; medium keeps the missed-win theme but broadens to longer forced mates (M2–M5) and missed winning tactics/material rather than strictly mate-in-1.

196.label: Top: leaves a major piece — usually the queen, or a rook grabbed by the enemy queen, often with check — en prise on an open line, frequently by removing its own guard/blocker; medium broadens to rooks and queens lost via knight forks, greedy pawn-grabs into bad trades, or plain undefended captures.

209.label: Top positions are uniformly passive king moves in pawn endgames that squander a critical tempo and lose the king-activity/centralization race; medium blurs the same tempo-wasting passivity onto other moves (pawn pushes like h3/a5, piece retreats like Bd1), occasionally crossing into outright material loss (Rxc3, skewer).

211.label: Top boards are tempo-losing or imprecise king/pawn moves in passed-pawn (king-and-pawn) endgames where the passer's escort/promotion technique slips; medium blurs into broader endgame-conversion errors — hung pieces, trapped bishops, premature pushes and king-safety lapses — and is heavily diluted by 0cp non-blunders.

194.label: Top positions are king moves that ignore a direct mating/winning attack (Kf1 instead of Kxh2, exposed Ke2, O-O-O into a pawn storm) — though some peak boards are tempo-loss/pointless checks; medium blurs into a wider class of king-exposing or piece-hanging moves (Kg2/Kd2/Kc1 into mate, g6, greedy Qxb2, hung knights) that walk into forced mate or drop material.

198.label: Top: in a lost/drawn position a rook (or queen) relocates and vacates the exposed king's last defense, allowing a forced mate or queen-losing check/fork; medium keeps the abandoned-defense-into-mate core but broadens to queen trades into hopeless endgames, illusory forks, and pawn moves that strip the final defender.

207.label: Top: in a clearly winning king-attack the player greedily grabs material (almost always a queen capture like Qxh1/Qxa8/Qxc1) instead of the forcing check or forced mate against the exposed king; medium broadens the same king-safety/conversion failure to any imprecise move — wrong check (Qb8+, Qh8+), king retreat into mate (Kh5, Kh8), pointless check (Rg1+) or quiet simplification — that throws away the precise forcing win.

218.label: Top boards are slow pawn moves (a3, e5, c5) that ignore an enemy attack or breakthrough while skipping a needed prophylactic hold; medium broadens to piece repositioning (Rfd8, Bg7) that abandons a key defender — in every case a non-forcing move lets the opponent's initiative turn decisive.

197.label: Top: king-safety blunders where a greedy capture or pawn push exposes the king / strips its shelter and is refuted by a forced attack; medium broadens to abandoning any key defender or playing a passive/greedy move that drops material or misses the only saving resource.

226.label: Top boards uniformly hang the QUEEN to a single attacker—either by moving it to an attacked square or ignoring it with an unrelated capture/development; medium boards keep the same one-ply self-hang mechanism but broaden the lost piece to rook/exchange, a forked knight, or even a promoted queen.

221.label: Top: in razor-thin positions with one good move, White/Black plays a natural active piece move (usually a rook lift) instead of the sole required quiet move—typically b3 to challenge an entrenched bishop on a2, or g6/b6 to keep an enemy minor piece restrained/trapped—letting that piece spring free; medium blurs to neglecting any single urgent only-move (challenging a bishop with h6/h3, the central capture, the right king square), more often a slow tempo-loss than a strict restraint, plus a stray true missed-material-win and a near-equal endgame, making the medium band genuinely mixed.

208.label: Top: clearly winning rook/pawn endgames thrown away by pushing a passed pawn or walking the king (sometimes hanging the rook to Kxf3) instead of the precise deflecting rook check that prevents a king blockade; medium keeps the same wrong-priority error but blurs across more move types (reflexive checks, tempo-wasting king/rook moves, a missed mate) at smaller magnitudes.

204.label: Top: a knight/bishop repositioning (or pawn grab) leaves a loose knight that drops after the opponent gains a tempo by deflecting the queen (Bg4/Nh5); medium broadens to any careless piece/pawn move whose vacated square or opened line lets the opponent win material—or shred the king with checks/mate—via a tempo-gaining reply.

214.label: Top: in a crushing position the player hangs a whole piece/rook outright (or skips a free capture/decisive shot), throwing the win away; medium broadens to softer squandering — purposeless checks, slow pawn pushes, inviting trades, or lesser tactical oversights (discovery/overload/back-rank, hung pawn) that merely shrink the winning edge.

233.label: Top: a winning king-and-pawn endgame squandered into a draw by a king/pawn move that misses the one decisive breakthrough or lock (g5, b4) or correct move-order/tempo, material staying safe (a missed win); medium broadens to general endgame imprecision in other piece configurations (knight, rook, bishop, queen), where the error is sometimes merely letting the advantage slip but sometimes actually drops material over the refutation.

223.label: Top: a developing or space-gaining move leaves the uncastled/central king on an open file or weakens key squares, punished by rook/queen penetration; medium keeps the exposed-king cases but broadens into loose pieces and pawn-grabs that walk into forks, pins, and traps.

225.label: Top: squandered a winning position with a routine capture/piece move instead of the decisive pawn break (f5/c5/e5/a4); medium broadens to any imprecise move that skips the win or lets the opponent's tactic (fork/hang/king-hit) strike.

222.label: Top: a 'simplifying' rook trade/recapture removes the back-rank (or f7) defender and gets the king mated, or loses material in the 2-3 move refutation; medium broadens to any move that strips a king's defender or makes a backfiring capture/king move, conceding a mating attack, dropping material, or squandering a winning position.

235.label: Top: hangs an under-defended central knight (almost always the d4/e5 knight, where Nxc6 was needed to resolve the tension) by developing/castling instead; medium broadens to hanging any minor piece in the opening — bishops too — via ignored captures, pins, removed defenders, or retreats into traps.

227.label: Top: queen checks — wrong move-order (Qd6+/Qe7+ instead of Rf1+) or queen left en prise — that throw away a forced mate; medium blurs to knight checks and other premature/missed-mate forcing moves (and one non-blunder), shifting from material-losing to merely win-skipping.

205.label: Constant across boards is a tempting active/repositioning piece move (often a bishop or rook, frequently 'attacking' the enemy queen/rook for tempo) that throws away a winning or equal position by ignoring the strongest forcing line; at the peak this is a clean MISSED win (overlooking a material-winning capture or forced mate while staying materially safe), whereas medium boards blur toward HANGING the moved piece outright (free captures, forks, trapped pieces, move-order errors).

228.label: Top: player overlooks a (usually bishop) move that pins/traps/directly attacks the enemy queen for a decisive win, choosing a routine recapture or passive move instead; medium broadens to other forcing wins — knight forks that net the queen, forced mates, and central pawn breaks.

232.label: Top: an attacking-looking non-capture ignores an en-prise enemy piece and hangs the exchange/rook (a winning capture was available); medium broadens to any natural move that overlooks the tactical refutation (pin, fork, mate, trapped piece), losing material, tempo, or the game.

230.label: Top boards hang a piece by abandoning a defender or stepping onto an undefended square—often enabling a rook/queen invasion on the 7th/back rank; medium boards blur into committal moves that instead surrender a key central square/outpost, trade into a lost endgame, or skip a winning capture.

248.label: Top: the queen vacates its post guarding the exposed king, inviting a decisive checking/mating attack (Qh5+, Qe3, Rf8+); medium broadens to any king-defender being removed — pawn shield (gxf6) or a defensive bishop/piece — leaving the king open to attack and material loss.

239.label: Top: trades off a dominant bishop for a knight (typically Bxc6/Bxc3, recaptured by pawn) and throws away a winning edge; medium broadens to any unfavorable minor-piece exchange (knight-for-bishop, bishop-for-bishop) and a few non-capturing moves that surrender the key piece/advantage.

236.label: Top: in a winning opening, plays a quiet developing/pawn move instead of capturing a knight hanging to a pawn (exf3/exf6-style free piece); medium broadens to missing smaller pawn-winning tactics, positional pushes that release central tension, and even some moves that hang own material.

241.label: At the peak, an aggressive/greedy move (often the queen) in an already-losing position deserts the king's last defender (or vacates a mating square), allowing an immediate forced checkmate; at medium the motif blurs from forced mate to also abandoning defenders of ordinary material or pawn-restraint, so the punishment is winning the dropped piece or squandering a won game rather than mate.

243.label: Top boards uniformly skip the forcing ...Bxf3/Bxf3 capture of the f3-knight (removing a defender to win material) in favor of a natural develop/castle/push; medium broadens to other mistimed or omitted critical exchanges (Bxc3, Rxc3, Bxf6-before-Nxd5) and quiet moves that allow the tactic, mixing in a few trapped/hung-piece cases.

234.chip: Missed winning tactic (knight retreat→any quiet move)
234.label: Top: a strongly-placed knight retreats from an advanced outpost (e4/g5/e5) and abandons a winning forcing combination, frequently an f7 sacrifice (Bxf7+/Bxf2+); medium broadens the move to any quiet opening move (pawns, bishops too) that squanders a winning edge, with the missed resource generalizing beyond f7 (Qxg7, Qxa1, Ng4, free pawn grabs) and several lines actually hanging own material rather than purely skipping a win.

245.label: Top: misses an immediate forced mate, almost always a clean mate-in-1 (or wrong-piece mate); medium: blurs to missing deeper forced mates (mate-in-3 through mate-in-16, even a queen-trap mate) and increasingly to walking the player's own king into a short forced mate via a greedy capture or loosening pawn/king move.

246.label: Top positions are uniformly a missed free capture of an undefended ROOK—the player pushed a quiet pawn or king move while the enemy rook sat hanging, letting it escape; medium blurs the captured piece (also a knight on bxc5) and mixes in a couple of own-piece hangs (premature e8=Q, Bxg5 into Kxg5), but the constant thread is skipping a one-move winning capture in an already-winning position.

229.chip: Skipped forcing check, own king exposed
229.label: Top: in a winning/holdable position the player skips the one decisive forcing queen-check (or makes a slow/greedy pawn-grab) and lets the enemy queen counterattack the exposed own king — perpetual or mate; medium broadens to equal/losing positions and to wrong checks or outright queen/piece hangs.

251.label: Top: spurns a direct, free undefended-queen capture (typically by a quiet king move); medium: still failing to win the queen but via a tactic/discovered-check/skewer or by capturing the wrong piece (minor or rook) instead.

247.label: At the peak these are losing rook/king-and-pawn endgames where the player mishandles a passed-pawn promotion race — hanging material to the promoting pawn/skewer, skipping a zwischenzug check, capturing the wrong target, or missing a mate (with some moves actually near-best); at medium it blurs into broader endgame tempo-loss and king/piece misplacement (king-rook/knight skewers, slow king marches) that drop material outside a strict promotion race.

242.chip: Hangs piece on open diagonal (top: knight w/check)
242.label: Top boards uniformly abandon a centralized knight (d5/d4) that's grabbed with a diagonal capture-check after the king/queen stops defending it; medium blurs to any piece hung on an open diagonal, sometimes without check, via lost pawn-support, or through a discovered attack.

268.label: Top: a slow 'chasing'/repositioning move (a4, h5, g6, axb4, Nxb4, Nd3) that ignores a one-move capture of a fully hanging queen (Nxb5, Nxg4, cxd6, cxb6, Bxb2, Bxa2, dxc3); medium broadens to missing a hanging minor piece (Rxa5, Rxb7) or otherwise squandering a clearly winning position with a positional/tempo-losing move instead of the single decisive continuation.

264.label: Top: in a completely won endgame a materially-safe move (often a quiet pawn/king move) skips capturing a free rook or a forced mate, staying winning but throwing away the immediate clincher; medium broadens to lesser conversion errors—greedy pawn-grabs or wrong-piece captures that miss the fastest/cleanest win (and a couple of near-best moves dilute the signal).

267.label: Top is rigid: a minor piece (almost always a knight, e.g. Nf6 vs e5 or Nc3 vs d4) left en prise to a pawn in the opening while the player makes an unrelated developing move, so the pawn just captures it for free; medium keeps the 'ignore-the-attack-and-hang-it' core but blurs the piece (now also bishops and even the queen) and the attacker/context (rook capture, failed sacrifices, king-safety/back-rank lapses).

269.label: Top boards almost uniformly miss a bishop shot (Ba6/Bb5/Bc4/Bf5) that wins the exchange by exploiting a queen-rook alignment on a light diagonal, the player instead choosing a slow positional move; medium boards blur the qualifier to any slow/non-forcing move that squanders the single critical resource — missing other material wins or even hanging pawns, pieces, or a back-rank mate.

259.label: Top: a king (or slow pawn) move goes the wrong direction in pawn/king endgames, squandering the decisive king march/infiltration or tempo race (mostly safe-but-missed-win); medium blurs to other passive or wrong-way pieces (knight to rim, passive rook/bishop) and tempo-losing moves that sometimes also hang a pawn or allow a tactic/mate.

273.label: Top: a greedy opening pawn capture/push (esp. queenside b2/b7) punished by a tempo-gaining recapture or zwischenzug; medium broadens to bishop/other captures grabbing a pawn that backfire tactically (Bxb2, hxg5, central d5/g7 pushes).

256.label: Top: in won endgames a king move or greedy capture ignores the opponent's dangerous passed pawn (move-order error), letting it promote and bleed material; medium broadens to other neglected endgame counterplay—abandoned blockaders, direct hangs, and a few missed forcing wins.

260.label: Top: a capture made with the wrong piece/order (or instead of the urgent recapture/defense) that overlooks an in-between move winning material; medium broadens to quiet or developing moves (castling, pawn push, queen sortie) that abandon a defender and hang material, with a few cases blurring into missed captures.

271.label: Top is dominated by self-weakening opening pawn pushes—especially ...f6/f3/f4 that expose the king (→Qh5+ Nxg6 / Qh4) or unsupport a central pawn—plus a few direct piece/queen hangs to a strong central knight; medium broadens to any loose-piece hang, allowed knight fork, trapped/greedy piece, or pure tempo/positional loss.

263.label: At the peak, slow king/rook/pawn moves in rook endgames squander a critical tempo (often skipping a tempo-gaining check), letting the opponent's forcing breakthrough — king march, passed-pawn push, or back-rank mate — decide; at medium it blurs into clearly missing a single forcing deflection/tempo check (or capture) that wins material or mate outright.

278.label: Top: passive move skips an immediate rook check on the exposed king (back-rank or uncastled) that wins a decisive tempo/material; medium: still misses a tempo-gaining check but broadens to queen/knight checks and blurs into general positional tempo loss.

272.label: Top: a tempo-losing 'harassing' check played just before the clean winning capture, letting the king escape and squandering the win; medium keeps the check-instead-of-capture skeleton but broadens to forcing checks that outright hang the piece or trade/sac it unfavorably.

280.label: Top boards almost all throw away a clearly winning position by voluntarily forcing/allowing a QUEEN trade that liquidates the attack into a flat/losing position (materially safe, just simplified); medium blurs to other advantage-dissolving simplifications/exchanges plus assorted tempo and positional slips that squander a won game without losing material outright.

284.label: Top: in a won queen endgame, a queen check or king move throws away a forced mate-in-1-to-3 by letting the enemy king escape; medium blurs to wrong-direction checks (now also rook/bishop moves) that miss not just mate but simply the fastest/material-winning conversion.

255.label: At the peak a quiet pawn/developing move in a won position ignores a free capture of the hanging enemy queen; at medium the same idea blurs to other hanging material (rook, the exchange, minor piece) and mixes in squandered forced mates, a few self-hangs, and tempo/positional drift.

286.label: Top boards uniformly leave a knight en prise to a direct pawn capture (almost always an f6/f3 knight grabbed by an advanced e-pawn via exf6/exf3); medium keeps the hung-knight-to-pawn theme but blurs the square and pawn (c6 knight to d5xc6, c3 to dxc3) and adds longer/tactical refutations plus one positional knight trade.

274.label: Top: hangs a major piece (rook/queen) in a dead-drawn endgame by moving another piece and leaving it en prise to a one-move capture; medium broadens to hanging a minor piece (bishop) exploited via an in-between check, with weaker tails drifting into missed-mate/tempo inaccuracies.

287.label: Top: capturing a rook (occasionally a queen) to 'simplify' liquidates a drawn/holdable position into a clearly lost K+P endgame; medium blurs to broader piece trades/captures in passed-pawn endgames (minor pieces, sometimes merely greedy or even the correct sac).

277.label: Top: a natural developing rook move to an open file (Rd8/Rc1/Rd1) skips a clear winning tactic—usually grabbing a loose/hanging enemy piece or a forcing shot (Nxf3+, Bxf2+, Qxc5); medium broadens to other quiet or committal moves (pawn pushes like e5/a4/b3, king moves) where the player instead hangs their OWN material to the opponent's reply, so the direction flips from 'missed win' at the peak to 'hangs material' at medium.

295.label: Top boards are winning king-and-pawn endgames where the king drifts to the edge/corner (Kh5, Kh6) or a premature pawn push (a5, g5) throws away the win into a draw/loss; medium blurs to marginal pawn pushes (g6) and near-neutral king moves (Kh4) where the eval loss is negligible or the move is actually best.

276.label: Top: a freshly developed bishop (Be6, mirror Be3) is hung to a Ng5+/Ng4+ knight check-fork that exploits the king stranded on f7/f2 and wins the piece; medium blurs to varied opening moves (g6, Na6, g3, e6) that neglect king safety and hang material to checking tactics (Qxd5+, Bb5+, even mate) rather than specifically a bishop-to-knight-fork.

275.label: Top: in clearly winning positions a quiet king/rook move ignores an immediate clean capture of an undefended enemy piece (queen/knight/bishop) or a forced mate; medium keeps the squandered-win theme but blurs to wrong-piece captures, missed mates, passive relocations, and drifting moves that hang one's own material to a fork or check.

282.label: Top: a slow defensive move or king-to-safety tuck in a sharp position declines a decisive capture/check (Rxf7, Qxa8+, Qb5+, perpetual Qg8+), either hanging the game/a piece or missing a clean win; medium keeps the same non-forcing-move theme but broadens to greedy grabs, king tucks into checks, ordinary hung pieces, and minor inaccuracies in already-lost positions, mostly just dropping material.

289.label: TOP: a greedy or careless capture/advance leaves White's (or Black's) QUEEN en prise—almost always recaptured by a pawn—trading the queen for far less; MEDIUM keeps the self-hang theme but blurs the piece (rook, bishop) and motive, adding king-safety captures where the recapture comes with check or opens lines, plus wrong-piece-trade and positional weakening.

296.label: Top: a winning side (opening) plays a quiet/flashy knight move that declines a free hanging-rook capture (Nf3 over Qxh5, Nfg5 over Nxe5); medium keeps the identical pattern—snubbing a clean free heavy-piece grab for a less forcing knight move—but the broader board set blurs into other skipped wins (queen via Nxb5, hung knight/forks, endgame tempo), so the unifying core is 'winning side passes up the strongest material capture.'

302.label: Top boards are uniformly clean back-rank ROOK mates (almost all mate-in-one, e.g. Rc1#/Rg1#/Rb8#) thrown away for a greedy or quiet move; medium keeps the 'missed forcing win' core but blurs the specifics — longer forced mates, mate-in-1 by other pieces (Rb2#), and material-winning tactics (forks, deflections, back-rank Qe1+/Qc8+), often still punishing an exposed king.

304.label: Top: in an already-lost position the player moves a key defender (usually the queen, or a pawn shielding the king like b3) off king-guard duty, converting 'losing-but-resisting' into a forced mate via checks; medium broadens to king-walks (Kf7) and back-rank abandonment (Qh3) that likewise expose the own king to a mating check sequence.

285.label: Top boards hang material or walk into mate by moving a piece off its defensive duty—unshielding the queen, vacating a mate-square guard, trading off a blockader (decisive piece/queen/mate loss); medium blurs to lesser and even marginal self-hangs, like shoving a passed pawn into a capture-with-tempo.

290.label: At the peak, the player makes a passive piece move that fails to attack an infiltrated enemy queen with tempo (Rg1/Rg8/Bg4 on the g-file), forfeiting the initiative; at medium it blurs to any tempo-losing move — slow retreats, king shuffles, prophylactic/greedy pawn moves — that surrenders momentum and, in roughly half the cases, also hangs material or allows a forcing material-winning reply.

303.label: Top: in a won opening the player reflexively retreats (or blocks the path to) an attacked bishop, missing Qxh5/Qxh4 which grabs the undefended attacking knight for free; medium blurs this into other quiet/retreating moves in winning positions that skip a winning capture, break, or push (still sometimes the same Qxh4 free-piece miss).

291.label: Top: a free/winnable enemy knight (frequently on d5) left uncaptured while the player makes a quiet pawn or developing move; medium broadens to knights on other squares and to allowing knight forks/incursions rather than capturing the knight.

301.label: Top boards are catastrophic conversion blunders in won/mating endgames—chiefly botched pawn promotions (underpromote to N/B or promote into a capture/decline promotion); medium boards keep the 'squandered winning endgame' theme but blur into subtler king-and-pawn technique like wrong-direction king moves, lost tempi, and missed opposition.

306.label: Top boards are razor-sharp K+P endgames where the player made a king move instead of the unique winning pawn push to the 7th, converting a won/mating position into a dead draw; medium blurs into general king-and-pawn conversion technique — often near-zero-loss inaccuracies or cases where the correct move was the king (opposition/blockade) rather than the push.

308.label: Top boards are uniformly an opening knight (rarely bishop) landing on f7 forking king+queen where only Kxf7 saves, so any other move (Qf6/Qe7/Qh4, Nb4, ...d6, ...Bb7) hangs the queen to Nxd8 or the d5-knight to Bxd5; medium blurs to any neglected forcing response—wrong king move instead of Kxf7, hanging a different piece (Bb5), ignoring tempo-gaining knight retreats/removing a defender, plus endgame tempo losses and a couple of missed-win sacrifices.

312.label: Top boards are all winning positions where a free undefended MAJOR piece (queen/rook) capture was overlooked for a quiet move; medium blurs to minor-piece targets and quiet moves that instead surrender the advantage or hang own material to mate/tactics.

319.label: Top: abandons a decisive attack on an exposed king (often skipping the crushing rook lift Rf3/Re3) via a slow recapture or material grab; medium broadens to throwing away any winning advantage, including endgames and pawn-promotion races, with a passive or greedy move.

320.label: Top: a bishop-takes-knight capture (Bxf6/Bxf3/Bxc3) that hangs own material—often the queen via a missed in-between threat (e.g. Bxf3 allowing Bxd8) or misses a winning capture (Bxh5); medium broadens to poor bishop trades and wrong-order captures (Bxf6/Bxc6/Bxc3) that squander a winning advantage without immediate material loss.

309.label: Top: a winning side ignores a free enemy QUEEN capture (and sometimes hangs its own queen by not taking first); medium broadens to any hanging piece — bishop/knight/rook/pawn — plus unsound sacrifices and wrong-capture choices, mixing 'missed win' and 'hung own'.

322.label: Top: in a lost position, a passive king/rook move collapses king safety and turns a defensible loss into forced mate; medium keeps the same losing-defense theme but broadens to outright hung pieces and pointless tempo moves.

311.label: Top: queen moves to aggressive attacking squares in sharp king-safety positions that either hang material or skip a forced mate; medium broadens to any piece (pawn/knight/bishop/rook/king) but keeps the same even split between hanging own material and missing a forced win/mate.

307.label: Top boards are uniformly a completely free, undefended enemy queen the player fails to grab in one move; medium keeps the queen as the central target but blurs to wins requiring a check, recapture, or correct move order—and occasionally another major piece such as a rook.

326.label: Top: in a totally won endgame the player played a quiet king/piece move (often Kx-elsewhere) instead of grabbing a hanging enemy ROOK for free (with a couple of queen/bishop cases); medium broadens to free-capturing other hanging pieces (bishop, exchange) and, more loosely, to skipping the simple winning capture/conversion entirely (wrong piece taken, wrong king route, missed pawn-race move).

323.chip: Opened line for enemy invasion (top: pawn captures)
323.label: Top: a greedy pawn/piece capture self-opens a file so the enemy rook invades (Rxa8, Rxh1+, Rxe8+, Rxd1#) to win material or mate; medium broadens to assorted line-opening or defender-abandoning moves enabling rook invasions, back-rank mates, and knight forks.

316.label: Top: clean missed back-rank queen checks (Qc1+/Qb1+/Qxd8+) winning material outright; medium blurs to rook checks (Rb1+), defensive perpetual checks, and quiet queen moves that instead hang material or walk into the opponent's mate.

324.label: At the peak, a queen (or key defender) move in an already-lost position abandons king/back-rank defense—typically declining the available saving queen trade—and walks into a forced checkmate; at medium activation it blurs into broader critical-moment blunders (passive, weakening, or structural moves) that throw away a winning or drawn position without an immediate mate.

328.label: Top boards are clean knight forks skewering the queen plus a rook/piece (Ng4, Nh5, Ne5, Nc6) that win material; medium blurs to a knight merely harassing the exposed queen with tempo (Nc5/Nb5 positional pressure, no clean fork).

330.label: At the peak, a passive/retreating move skips a forcing shot—usually a check or queen strike against an exposed, uncastled king (Qh5+, Bb5+, Nd3+, Qd5); at medium it broadens to any missed win, including quiet captures of hanging pieces, knight forks, and central pawn breaks.

329.label: Top boards are 'patzer-check' rook moves (Rh4+, Rxg2+, Rb1+, Re2+, Rxb2+, Rxh2+) where the checking rook is simply recaptured, hanging the whole rook and converting a win into a loss/draw; medium boards blur the outcome — the same forcing rook check or trade-offer instead loses only the exchange (fxg3), a tempo, or a winning king-and-pawn endgame rather than the entire piece.

313.label: At the peak, a quiet developing or flank-pawn move in a winning/drawn opening passes up a forcing win that exploits the enemy king (a knight fork like Nxc7+, or a winning check/grab such as Qh4+, Qa5+, Qxb2); at medium the pattern blurs as the same slow, non-forcing move instead surrenders the initiative or actively allows the OPPONENT's tactic (often a knight fork like Nc7+/Nxc2+) and hangs material, flipping the direction from 'Missed' to 'Hangs'.

332.label: Top boards hang a knight—moved into a capture or stranded by vacating its defender—for a clean full-piece loss; medium keeps the hung-undefended-piece theme but broadens to any unit (bishop, pawn) and to king-safety/structure collapses where material follows.

334.label: Top boards almost all squander a winning endgame by pushing a pawn straight into promotion where it's immediately captured (hanging the new queen); medium boards blur to hanging any piece or pawn to an overlooked capture/tactic while ahead, plus a few purely positional concessions.

341.label: Top boards hang a rook for free to the enemy king's adjacent capture; medium boards broaden to rook captures made without the winning intermediate check (skipped zwischenzug), losing material or the stronger continuation.

335.label: Top: king-safety blunders that ignore a critical defense and walk into a FORCED MATE (often a queen/bishop battery, e.g. Qg2#, or a king-march mating net); medium: same 'ignored the decisive threat' structure but the punishment blurs from forced mate to any material-winning tactic (discovered attacks, queen traps, kicked pieces, lost endgames).

327.label: Top: a knight steps back (usually Nd2/Ne2) to challenge a central enemy knight but walks into a tactic—often an Nxf2+ fork or capture-with-tempo—losing material; medium blurs both the piece (some pawn/bishop moves creep in) and the direction, splitting between hanging material and passive knight retreats that merely miss a winning knight jump (Nd4/Nf2/Ne3).

338.label: Top: critical tempo loss in a sharp pawn race, nearly always failing to push the passed pawn (esp. ...f3) and letting the opponent blockade it; medium broadens to any passive/slow move squandering the key tempo—wrong-way king moves, move-order slips, abandoning a passer's support, even defensive retreats that hang material or allow mate.

344.label: Top: in an equal opening a knight/queen (or bishop) move abandons the c4 bishop—or symmetrically the e4 knight (e5/c5 mirror)—to a free ...dxc4/dxe4 capture because the forced Bd3 was skipped; medium blurs to broader central minor-piece mishandling—failing to capture/exchange or defend the e4/e5 knight, mixing hangs with a few missed captures.

333.label: Peak mixes a premature pawn push hanging the connected passer (rook endgame) with king missteps that surrender control and lose a pawn over 2-3 moves in lost endgames; the medium/typical case narrows to exactly the g4-g3 push splitting the passed pawns in a lost rook endgame.

347.chip: Hangs material to overlooked tactic (broadens positional)
347.label: Top: a quiet, non-capturing move (often a bishop relocation/retreat) leaves a piece or the exchange hanging to an overlooked knight tactic—fork, discovered attack, or removed defender (Nxf8, Nf6+, Nf3+, Nxe7+); medium keeps the 'passive move ignores the position's demand' theme but blurs the outcome, broadening to positional/structural neglect (dropping a pawn, en-passant passer, tempo loss) and even missed wins, so it's no longer purely a hung-piece-to-tactic feature.

350.label: Top: winning endgames where player skips an immediate king-capture of an undefended rook (often Kxh2 in a promotion race) for a useless check; medium broadens to skipping any precise forcing move (tempo-check, pawn break) in a favorable endgame.

349.label: Top boards uniformly skip the tactical Bxd6/Bxd3 capture of an undefended dark-squared bishop that wins a full piece in a won opening (player instead develops a knight or retreats), while medium blurs into other passed-up material-winning tactics (Nd6 outpost, Ng5 hitting f7, Bd3) plus a few borderline multi-move material drops and positional/endgame errors.

343.label: Top: a greedy ROOK capture (often eliminating a king-defender or opening a line) walks straight into immediate checkmate; medium broadens the captured piece to any (rook/bishop/queen) and the punishment to a wider mix — hanging-queen/exchange recaptures, forks, or back-rank mate.

353.label: Top: hangs a piece (almost always a knight) in the opening by advancing/recapturing onto an undefended central square like e5 or d4 where a pawn or Nf3 grabs it for free; medium blurs both the piece (queen/bishop, leaving a stranded knight) and the phase/direction, adding king-safety collapses and missed material-winning shots (e.g. Kd3 vs Qf2) in the middlegame and endgame.

346.label: At the peak, a queen move or capture hangs the queen itself or a piece it was guarding (or grabs a pawn and gets trapped), throwing away a winning position; at medium strength this blurs to other pieces (knight, bishop) and includes some missed wins/mates.

354.label: Top boards are uniformly early queen sallies to b3/b6 (eyeing b7/b2 and d5/d4) that either hang the queen outright or squander a winning edge by ignoring a stronger continuation; medium broadens to queen sorties to other exposed squares (a5, b4, b5, g4/g5) punished by tempo-losing kicks or simple capture, with a few non-queen tempo-wasters mixing the direction between hanging material and merely losing time/missing a win.

355.label: Top: a quiet king/bishop/queen move in a won position hangs a major piece to an immediate refutation (often missing the winning ...Rxh5 queen-capture); medium broadens to positional/king-safety moves that squander the advantage without a clean material hang.

357.label: Top: a queen checking-capture (overwhelmingly Qxf8+) that surrenders the queen for a rook or nothing; medium broadens to other losing queen moves — a Scholar's-style Qxf7+ hang, a quiet Qa4 that allows Nf6+ mate, and even a passive Qf8 that MISSES a knight fork, mixing hang-the-queen with missed-win.

348.label: Top boards almost all involve a quiet/developing move that leaves the QUEEN en prise (or that skips capturing the enemy queen) in a winning position; medium boards blur in both directions — hanging or failing to win other material (rooks, pawns, the exchange) and missing forcing checks/mates rather than just queen tactics.

368.label: Top is constant on unsound bishop sacrifices/moves giving up a piece for little (esp. Bxf7+ that the king just takes); medium blurs to any piece (knight, queen, rook) moved off a defending/blocking square or into a hang, losing material or allowing mate.

363.label: Top boards constantly squander a winning passer by playing a slow pawn/bishop move (typically missing the forcing Rb1+ rook-sac promotion), letting White capture the key passed pawn; medium blurs to general passed-pawn/promotion mishandling—wrong escort, over-pushing, or skipping king centralization, sometimes in pawn endgames.

373.label: Top: from a winning position, played a quiet/non-best move that squandered a FORCED CHECKMATE (very often a mate-in-one, frequently back-rank); medium keeps the 'overlooked the kill in a winning position' theme but blurs the win from strict mate to any decisive continuation — queen-winning tactics, sustaining the mating attack, or the single strongest move — including a couple of cases where the chosen move actively loses tempo.

361.label: Top boards consistently walk into a knight fork/attack that targets the exposed queen (often queen+minor); medium broadens to knight forks hitting the king, a bishop, or just a loose pawn instead of the queen, with a few missed-win outliers in both tiers.

369.label: Top: an automatic simplifying capture (queen or rook, often with check) in a won endgame that grabs material but skips a faster forced mate while staying winning; medium blurs the line — the same greedy recapture sometimes actually loses (walking into a knight fork on b5/a3 or a pawn recapture that hangs the rook into a draw), and several flagged captures are no real error at all.

365.label: Top: in dead-lost king-and-pawn endgames the king steps the wrong direction and loses the critical pawn/tempo race (often near-0 cp since already lost); medium blurs to winnable or even winning positions—and occasional knight/bishop moves—where the same wasted tempo actually squanders real material or the win.

367.label: Top: a king move (usually 'centralizing') in a drawn/lost endgame that ignores the ONE saving only-move — typically a capture (Kxb6/Kxf8/Nxh5/Rxd3) or stopping promotion/fork — causing a catastrophic swing; medium: the same king/pawn-in-endgame pattern blurs into minor tempo/king-activity inaccuracies that merely worsen an already-decided position.

374.label: Top boards abandon a decisive/forced-mate attack with a slow or misdirected move so the enemy king escapes and counterattacks; medium blurs this into a wrong attacking grab that also drops material, but the constant is squandering a winning king-side attack.

386.label: Top boards uniformly miss a one-move free capture of a completely undefended ROOK (Bxa8, Bxg7, Nxe5, etc.); medium boards keep the same 'grab the hanging piece' theme but blur to also include an undefended queen (Nxe7) and cases of snatching a lesser piece/pawn instead of the free rook (Qxb3 over Qxa6, Nxf6 over Nxc5).

384.label: Top boards skip an available forced mate — almost always a back-rank mate with the king walled in by its own pawns — while medium blurs into missing other winning tactics (forks, passed-pawn breaks) or even moving a defender off the back rank and allowing the opponent's mate.

375.chip: Greedy wing-pawn grab squanders win (often rook)
375.label: Top: an active/dominant rook abandons its central post to greedily chase a wing pawn (or skips a winning simplification/capture), converting a winning eval to drawn/worse; medium broadens to other pieces (knight, king, bishop, pawn) and to general 'wrong-target/wrong-plan' moves that abandon the critical resource and allow tactics or positional collapse.

360.label: Top: a decisive endgame pawn push that loosens own king/structure and is refuted by a capture or 3rd-rank check, often losing a pawn or handing the opponent a passed pawn; medium blurs to milder positional/tempo-losing pushes and even a few non-pawn king/knight moves that walk into a pawn capture or check.

364.label: Top: a knight sortie attacking the enemy queen that backfires—the queen retreats to a SUPERIOR square, leaving the knight misplaced/trapped and bleeding tempo or material; medium broadens to any over-aggressive minor-piece jump to an unsupported square (outpost grab, sac) that simply hangs or drops material, not necessarily targeting the queen.

391.label: Top: a developing move drops a full piece into an immediate free capture, very often straight into an enemy pawn's path (Nc3 vs d4, Nf6 vs e5) or onto an undefended square; medium broadens to any early material loss—pieces hung to queen/knight, trapped or forked knights, and dropped pawns.

382.label: Top: a natural-looking 'safe/improving' move (g6, Rd1, Nd5, Ne8, Qxd4) that pulls the sole defender of the king's shelter or a key piece, hanging material or allowing a forced mate/attack the move ignored; medium blurs to any overlooked tactic — direct hangs, greedy recaptures, queen-deflections, plus a few materially-safe moves that miss a win (Rxd3, Nbxd4, promotion).

380.label: At the peak: passive king/rook repositioning in already-lost queen-vs-rook(+pawn) endgames that lets the rook get trapped (the repeated Rf6 by a king march) or the king mated; at medium it blurs to broader worse-position defensive slips — king-safety pawn weaknesses (g6/f5/a5) and other passive moves that concede material or a mating attack — and the top set is noisy (several flagged moves are actually best or near-best).

362.label: Top: passive retreats/relocations that decline a strong capture (often Rxb5/Rxc4) or fail to stop an opponent's passed pawn, forfeiting initiative in endgames; medium broadens to passive moves that outright hang the moved piece (knight/rook/pawn walks into a capture or abandons a defender).

385.label: Top: from a winning position the player skips a decisive queen capture/sacrifice—usually Qxf7/Qxd8/Qxc7 exploiting a back-rank or overloaded/undefended defender to win a rook or force mate; Medium blurs the direction, adding hung own pieces and walking into the opponent's king-side mating tactics (plus a couple of pure positional drops).

390.chip: Hangs material in faulty trade (often rook, king attack)
390.label: Top boards are constant: a capture/trade (usually a rook) that hangs the player's own king to a forcing mating/checking attack (Qxf6+, e8=Q+, Nh3+, Qxh2#); medium blurs this into any move — pawn pushes, piece development, or trades — that simply hangs material or drops a piece to a tactical refutation (removal-of-defender, attack on overextended piece) rather than a pure king hunt.

405.label: Top boards are king moves that march straight into a forced mating net while ignoring a free defensive queen capture (Rxh1/Bxf3/Kxg8 etc.); medium blurs to other king/rook/pawn moves that simply lose material or skip a saving resource without an immediate forced mate.
