1655.label: Top boards self-weaken the king and allow a forcing queen check that forces mate (often Qxa6+ on the queenside king); medium broadens to checks (Qxe6+, Qxd4+) that merely win material rather than deliver mate.

1652.label: Top boards uniformly skip a material-winning queen check on the c-file (Qxc3+/Qxc6+) against an uncastled e1-king; medium boards broaden to other forcing winning shots — knight forks, skewers, mate-in-one, and recaptures-with-check.

1636.label: Top: opening moves that expose the king or the f7/e6 squares to an active queen (Qh5+Bc4 battery, opened diagonals/e-file), refuted by a queen check, capture, fork or even Scholar's-mate; medium blurs this to any phase where moving a piece abandons a defender and drops a piece or pawn to any attacker (queen/bishop/rook), with a couple of missed-win deflections mixed in.

1661.label: Top: played a tempting queen check (frequently a capture-with-check) that stays winning but throws away an immediate forced mate ('sees a check, gives a check'); medium broadens to rook/pawn checks and sometimes to missing a winning continuation rather than strictly a mate.

1660.label: Top boards hang an undefended bishop on an aggressive opening sortie — overwhelmingly the anti-fianchetto pokes Bh6/Ba6 (plus a Bxf7 sac and mirror-image Bh3); medium narrows to the pure Ba6/Bh6 fianchetto-prevention bishop that drops for free.

1657.chip: Hangs piece on flashy check (often rook)
1657.label: Top boards are rook sacrifices/checks that simply get recaptured (Kxd2, Kxg2, fxg6, Bxh3), hanging the rook and squandering a winning attack or even a forced mate; medium broadens to queen and bishop checks/captures (Rg5+, Bxd5, Qc3+, Rxh2+) plus quiet hanging moves and endgame misconversions, all throwing away a won position via a flashy-but-refuted move.

1618.label: Top: a natural developing move ignores an aggressively-posted enemy knight (usually Ng5 hitting f7, punished by the missed ...h6) or a knight-fork threat; medium keeps the 'developing move ignores an opening threat' skeleton but broadens the refuting tactic to bishop grabs, Greek-gift, pins, forks and back-rank shots, often hanging material.

1665.label: Top: in a won position the player ignores a trivial capture of an undefended enemy QUEEN (usually moving its own queen away); medium broadens the free piece to rooks/bishops and occasionally has the player hang its own piece instead of grabbing the win.

1667.chip: Hangs king to mate (material at medium)
1667.label: Top: a move exposes own king to a forced checkmate—typically by removing the lone defender of a back-rank/key square or stepping into a decisive check; medium keeps the same 'ignored the killer threat' idea but broadens from mate to plain material loss (exchange, piece, queen) via captures-with-check, deflections, or file invasions.

1664.label: Top boards are premature pawn pushes that throw away a won pawn endgame (win→draw, the push usually hanging the pawn or breaking the winning chain); medium blurs to include king moves and other tempo-losing endgame moves that squander the win, with several false positives where the flagged move is actually optimal.

1663.label: Top: a non-capturing pawn push in a losing/drawn pawn endgame that dissolves a locked or held pawn structure, handing the opponent a decisive passed pawn or king penetration; medium broadens to king/minor-piece moves that abandon a blockade or sole defender, still hastening the loss.

1677.label: Top boards are uniformly a winning-position miss of a forcing sacrifice/deflection/fork that wins the enemy QUEEN (player instead plays a quiet/safe move); medium keeps the 'squandered tactical win' core but broadens the prize to a rook/exchange, full piece, or forced mate—and occasionally the passive move also hangs own material.

1672.label: Top: a (usually knight) maneuver to a passive, purposeless square that wastes tempo while staying materially safe, missing the active/centralizing/blockading post; medium blurs to other pieces (rook, bishop, pawn) and to moves that outright hang the piece or abandon a defended one, often with king-safety undertones.

1673.label: Top: in a lost position, declines the only-move queen capture/trade and plays a non-defensive move, accelerating a forced mating net; medium broadens to assorted defensive lapses (back-rank mate, hanging bishop, missed only-move) where the queen-trade theme dissolves and one fire is even the best move.

1668.label: Top: from a won middlegame, White/Black makes a queen capture that trades queens prematurely, defusing a winning attack/initiative into equality (often a missed forcing intermezzo or fork); medium broadens to the same winning-position queen capture but now loses material outright—hanging the queen on an attacked square or capturing a defended/recheckable piece (sometimes a rook), so the SEE 'trade' becomes a true blunder.

1654.label: Top boards uniformly leave a free undefended enemy QUEEN on the board and the player plays anything else (a quiet move, or one that even drops their own queen); medium keeps the winning-position theme but blurs to missed free rooks, missed forced mates/promotions, and queens lost via forks or discovered checks rather than simply hanging.

1653.label: Top: in a clearly won endgame a quiet king/non-forcing move skips a free or decisive capture (usually a hanging rook), squandering the win; medium: king moves to inferior squares that merely lose tempo or walk into forks/passed-pawn breaks, blurring into broader endgame-conversion and king-safety errors.

1666.label: Top: queen moves (passive retreats or unfavorable trades) abandon a dominant post and throw away a winning/holding advantage; medium broadens to any piece (rook, pawn, king) relocating to an inferior square that misses a forced win or allows a decisive refutation.

1691.label: Top: passing up an immediate capture of an undefended/loose rook (Qxe8); medium broadens to missing a rook-winning capture (via overload/queen-trade tactics like Qxf1, Qxd2) while opting for a safe but lesser pawn grab.

1678.label: Top: opening positions where a quiet developing/repositioning move (Bd2, Bf4, Qf3, Qc7) skips the one forcing winning shot — overwhelmingly a Qg4-type strike on g7/e4 or a Bxf7+ break against the uncastled king; medium: broadens to any phase, where a plausible natural move squanders a winning/equal eval by missing the single precise continuation (with a few cases tipping into outright hangs/mates).

1671.label: Top boards are quiet moves that let the opponent harass a piece (queen/knight) with tempo for positional/advantage loss; medium boards broaden to allowing knight forks and double attacks that win material outright.

1693.label: At the peak it fires on a tempting check/capture/king-move that throws away an immediate forced mate (overwhelmingly mate-in-1); at medium it blurs to squandering a decisive winning (or holdable) advantage more broadly — longer forced mates, win-to-draw tempo losses, and the odd hung piece — in already won or equal positions.

1689.label: At the peak the player abandons a concrete forced checkmate—typically by grabbing a pawn or shuffling a rook off its mating post (greedy/tempo-loss); at medium the identical self-defeating choice merely squanders a decisive winning advantage (mate distance balloons or a big eval drop) and broadens to non-grab errors like positional, endgame, and passed-pawn misjudgments.

1694.label: Top boards are unsound Bxf2+/Bxh2+ bishop-sacrifice checks that hang a bishop for a pawn in the opening when a simple capture won material; medium boards lose the bishop-check signature entirely and blur into assorted material-dropping blunders—greedy queen grabs, undefended knights/queens, hung exchanges, even king-safety mates and missed forced mates.

1684.label: Top: a knight grabs a defended central pawn (Nxd5/Nxe4/Nxe5) and is simply recaptured, losing a minor piece for one pawn; medium keeps the opening one-move material loss but broadens beyond the greedy knight-grab to Bxf7+ bishop sacs, hung queen sorties (Qg5/Qc5) and trapped/overextended pieces.

1695.label: Top boards are opening pawn thrusts (...d6/...g5/...b5) that attack an enemy bishop but hang material to a stronger bishop capture or sac (Bxg7, Bxg5, Bxf7+); medium broadens to challenging/attacking ANY piece for a tempo — bishops met by pieces, plus queen/knight chases and trade-offers — that still drop material or concede structure.

1680.label: Top boards uniformly decline a clean, free enemy ROOK capture (Nxd2, Kxh7, dxe6, Bxd1, Nxc7) in favor of a quiet king-walk or pawn push; medium keeps the missed-rook core but blurs it to lesser/exchange captures (Nxe7, Rxf6-vs-Kxa7) and rook grabs needed to avert mate (Kxf3, Rxe5), plus a few pure king-safety/move-order lapses.

1687.label: Top: a forced win (often mate) is thrown away by a quiet king move that walks into a mating net or ignores a hanging enemy queen instead of grabbing it; medium broadens to pawn pushes, queen retreats and move-order slips that expose the king or drop material, downgrading the win rather than mating instantly.

1704.label: Top: a king-safety lapse (usually a king walk like Kc7/Kd2/Kf3, or pulling a defender) that lets the opponent crash through with a forced mating check; medium: the same king-exposure idea but blurs from forced mate to merely losing material or squandering the advantage via decisive checks (Kh7, Kf1, Kf5).

1705.label: At the peak it's king-safety collapse — a committal forward move (Rff4, Nf6, f4) that abandons a defender and leads to back-rank mate or a shattered kingside; at medium it blurs into generic material loss/inactivity, hanging a minor piece or pawn (d3) or burning a tempo with a non-defensive rook move (Rb4).

1702.label: Top: a natural developing move (usually a knight) leaves an advanced/passed central enemy pawn (e6/d6/e5/d4) uncaptured and is punished by that pawn advancing with check or enabling a fork (exf7+, Nb5, Qe2+); medium blurs into neglecting pawn tension generally — kingside storms and en-passant breaks (g5/f4), plus skipped free pawn grabs — played with assorted pieces and with more purely positional rather than direct material fallout.

1709.label: At the peak the player squanders a forced mate or crushing kingside attack by grabbing material or playing a quiet/passive move; at medium it broadens to missing simpler material-winning tactics and shades into outright hanging a piece (or walking into mate).

1710.label: Top: hangs a rook by making a quiet pawn/rook move while the rook is attacked or under file tension (typically failing to play the mandatory Rxa1/Rxh7/Rxd1 exchange first), letting it be captured for free; medium broadens to hanging the queen too (Qd5, Be3, Qe2) and to king/king-safety moves that drop major-piece material or walk into a 2-3 move mating/winning refutation.

1696.label: At the peak the player makes a slower pawn-push or king/rook move in a clearly won endgame instead of the engine's immediate capture (usually ~0cp, not really a blunder); at medium this blurs into king/pawn moves that genuinely throw away the win or draw via wrong king route, structural pawn errors, or abandoned defense.

1688.label: At the peak the player is in a dead-drawn endgame and skips an elementary knight-capture of a hanging queen (king/knight move instead, own material stays safe = missed win); at medium the pattern blurs badly — the 'typical' boards (Bxg7, dxe5) are greedy/positional blunders that lose material or equality rather than clean missed captures, so the unifying thread is only 'squandered a balanced/drawn position by a material misjudgment.'

1711.label: At the peak the just-moved piece (most often a bishop or queen, plus a king walking into mate) is dropped on a square where it's captured for free in a single ply; medium positions blur this to material lost over a 2-3 move refutation, a different/unmoved piece left hanging (e.g. the a4-rook after Nf3), and bleed into skipped forced wins and tempo-losing pushes.

1712.label: Top boards: a routine developing move skips the Bg5/Bg4 bishop shot that wins the exchange off an exposed enemy queen (usually on f6/f3) in the opening; medium blurs into squandering any winning position — still mostly missed material-winning tactics, but now also self-inflicted hangs via forks, king-safety lapses, and undefended minors.

1721.label: Top: a greedy capture of the enemy queen/major piece (Rxe8, Qxd5, Kxf7) ignores a forcing in-between shot—almost always a back-rank check that mates or wins material; medium blurs to any natural capture or trade that overlooks a stronger zwischenzug/intermediate move, where the refutation is no longer specifically a back-rank mate and the cost is sometimes just a missed bigger win rather than lost material.

1722.label: Top: in a won position the player chooses a safe/routine move and misses a knight fork delivered WITH CHECK that wins a rook or the exchange; medium keeps the 'missed forcing win' theme but blurs the piece/motif — other forks (pawn, queen, rook), forcing checks, and recaptures that skip the cleanest win.

1724.label: Top boards are pawn-advance checks that fix the structure or hand the enemy king a key infiltration/blockade square (Kf4/Ke4/Kc6); medium broadens to rook/knight checks (Rf8+, Nd5+, Ne7+) that release a confined king or just waste a tempo, the forcing-check bias squandering a winning or drawn endgame rather than hanging material.

1725.label: Top: in an already-losing position, a king-exposing or back-rank move converts it into a forced mate (king safety collapse is constant at the peak); medium broadens to any move that merely accelerates an already-lost game — small cp/mate-distance slips, endgame inaccuracies, or a hung piece — where the 'mistake' is often just continued flailing in a hopeless position.

1727.label: Top: clearly winning pawn endgames squandered to a draw by a slow king/pawn move instead of the one decisive pawn break (b4 or f5) or correct break move-order; medium blurs to general precision/tempo losses — slow king moves, wrong recaptures, and even missed tactics/forks — that throw away an advantage.

1726.label: Top: a knight jumps to a phantom central outpost (e4/d5) and is won by an exchange that strips its lone pawn-defender; medium keeps the same 'capture–recapture–loose target' refutation but broadens to bishops/queens (and a few missed captures/forks) hung the same way.

1730.label: Top: a natural recapture/capture of an intruding piece hangs own material by skipping the tempo-gaining zwischenzug or correct move-order (often a queen/pawn recapture); medium blurs to broader tactical oversights from grabbing material — walking the king into knight forks, opening the king, and missing winning shots or even mate-in-one.

1715.chip: Hangs knight skipping tempo check (or fork)
1715.label: Top boards are almost all endgames where the player ignored a tempo-gaining knight check (Nf4+/Ne4+/Nd5+/Nc6+) that would rescue their own hanging knight or hold the king-and-pawn endgame, and instead played a passive king/pawn move that drops the knight; medium broadens to other forcing resources—knight forks (Nd6+/Nd3+), bishop/pawn checks (Be4+/g4+), quiet saving retreats (Ne5/Nf2)—and increasingly includes materially-safe moves that merely miss a win rather than literally hang a piece.

1706.label: Top: near-equal openings where a passive bishop/knight development (instead of the ...d5 central break) is refuted either by a direct capture (Bc5/Nf5/Bg4 hung) or a tempo-gaining central pawn push (d5/e5); medium blurs across phases and error-types, becoming any quiet/misplacing move that skips the one critical pawn break or capture, sometimes trapping or hanging the piece rather than just ceding the center.

1733.label: Top: a pawn push or exchange in a pawn endgame that dissolves the player's own passed pawn or majority (the pawn gets recaptured, surrendering the queenside/kingside trump) — often even the engine-best move in an already-lost position; medium keeps the 'wrong endgame plan' theme but blurs to non-pawn moves (misplaced king like Kf7/Kg5, tempo-wasting, even a queen sortie) that squander winning or holding chances rather than strictly dissolving a passer.

1737.chip: Hangs piece to overlooked tactic (often opening f7-fork)
1737.label: Top: opening blunders that ignore an f7/f2/c7 knight-fork or mating shot and hang a piece (royal forks, Qxf7#/Qxf2#); medium broadens to overlooking the opponent's tactical reply more generally—middlegame piece hangs, allowed mates and discovered attacks, even slower positional/tempo lapses across all phases.

1741.label: Top: a knight lunges to a rim square (a4/a5/h4/h5/g4) to harass a bishop and is captured for free; medium broadens to non-rim knight sorties against a bishop that backfire to tactics/king exposure, plus a few unrelated tempo-loss and missed-win moves.

1708.label: Top: a quiet opening developing/repositioning move (…d6, …Nf6, …Qd7, Qe1) declines capturing or recapturing an en-prise intruding bishop, leaving the player effectively down a piece; medium broadens the intruder to knights/rooks/pawns, reaches the middlegame, and sometimes the quiet move also hangs material to a fork.

1734.label: Top boards all miss a forcing knight check that launches a winning/mating combo; medium keeps the 'skipped a forcing win' core but blurs to bishop checks, rook swings, and even quiet/greedy alternatives rather than a pure knight check.

1747.label: Top: clearly winning endgames thrown away by a slow pawn push or wrong-direction king move instead of the precise king centralization/activation (Kd4/Ke3/Kf4/Ke5); medium keeps the 'imprecise endgame move squanders the result' core but blurs the specific fix—now opposition/outflanking errors, missed promotion/mate control, a hung pawn, or a missed tactic.

1752.label: Top boards almost always hang the QUEEN—typically by moving its sole defender or grabbing material, leaving it captured by a knight (frequently with check); medium keeps the 'left a piece en prise' core but blurs to any piece (rook, bishop, even pawn) taken by assorted attackers.

1748.label: Top: in a winning position the player chooses a slow, non-forcing move (Bb3, Rhg1, h5, Kc6) and skips a decisive forcing shot — most often a 7th-rank rook check (Rd7+/Ra7+) or tactic that wins material; medium keeps the 'passive move missing the best' core but blurs the target, missing material grabs (Qxb7, Rc8, Bxf3), positional improvements (Bb2, c4), or king activation (Kf2) rather than a pure forcing combination.

1746.label: Top: a clearly winning position is thrown away by a tempting queen check, capture, or auto-promotion that skips a forced mate or decisive material win; medium broadens to narrower edges blown by pawn grabs, speculative sacrifices, wrong-piece checks, and patzer checks that miss the only winning tactic or hang material.

1743.label: Top: a knight grabs a central pawn or centralizes (often deserting an f6/f3 defensive post), hanging a minor piece to a tactical refutation; medium blurs to any premature piece sortie or grab (bishop, pawn) that loses material or, occasionally, skips a stronger win.

1750.label: Top: a bishop grabs a piece on f3/f6/e2/e7 and is cleanly recaptured by the queen, needlessly trading off a strong/dominant bishop (or missing mate) and squandering a clear advantage; medium broadens to rooks/knights/pawns also capturing or moving into a recapture (gxf3, Nxd2, even allowing a fork), the same advantage-releasing trade/capture.

1744.label: At the peak: clearly-winning positions where a natural recapture or quiet developing/centralizing move throws away a concrete forcing win — most often a forced mate (boards 1,2,6,7) or a decisive material grab (trapped knight, hanging queen, winning fork); at medium it blurs toward less-decisive positions where a natural pawn push or recapture overlooks the precise line and merely squanders the edge or hangs a pawn/piece to the opponent's tactic, so the direction drifts from 'missed own knockout' to 'allowed their resource'.

1754.label: Top boards hang a rook/queen (or the exchange) to a forcing check — discovered or intermediate — that exploits an exposed king; medium blurs into knight forks, immediate mate, plain piece-hangs and even a missed win.

1745.label: Top boards uniformly fail to capture an enemy minor piece infiltrated to h6/h3 in the castled king's pawn-shield (the winning gxh6/gxh3 or Bxh6); medium blurs to ignoring kingside threats and free captures generally (Greek-gift Kxh7, hanging rooks, promotion), often hanging own material rather than missing a capture.

1757.chip: Hangs material to centralized queen (often rook)
1757.label: Top boards are quiet opening moves that hang the h8 rook (or a piece/pawn) to a centralized White Qd4 raking the open long diagonal; medium blurs to any material dropped to an active enemy queen in the opening (Qxg2, Qxh8, Qe4+, Qb5+ fork), with a couple of non-queen tempo/missed-win cases mixed in.

1759.label: Top: a critical enemy passed pawn one step from queening is ignored — the player fails to blockade it (Rf1/Rd8) or capture it (Rxa2/Kxa2) and loses immediately to promotion; medium keeps the promoting-passer theme but broadens the cause to wrong recaptures (cxb3), vacated blockade/control squares (Re1, Re4, Rd2), and passive king play (Kg2), with a couple of king-safety/back-rank breaks blurring the edge.

1756.label: Top boards trade or sacrifice the rook that shields an already-exposed king (Rxe8/Rf8+/Rh1) or abandon it (g6, Kh8), walking into forced mate; medium broadens to any misplaced/removed defender — a wandering queen (Qc8, Qb8), a knight blocker/guard (Nf2, gxf6), or a king-weakening pawn move — that concedes a decisive attack or simply drops material.

1753.label: Top: a tempo-gaining move attacking an enemy piece (usually the queen) cleanly hangs own material to an immediate capture or zwischenzug; medium broadens to pawn-kicks of a bishop/knight (h6, h3) where the loss is structural or multi-move, plus a few non-harassing king-safety/missed-mate lapses.

1770.chip: Hangs piece in won endgame (often major)
1770.label: Top boards constantly hang a queen or rook—frequently via a pointless check the enemy king/piece just captures—throwing away a totally won endgame; medium blurs the piece to minor pieces (knight/bishop) and a few squandered conversions/technique slips.

1758.label: Top: a slow pawn (or piece) move to chase/kick an enemy piece—usually a3/h3—that squanders a winning position by ignoring a forcing queen fork or hanging-piece capture; medium broadens to assorted tempo-wasting natural moves (h5, a6, a4, g4, g5, c6, premature O-O) that instead allow a tactical refutation or weaken the king, blurring 'missed win' into 'allowed/hung material'.

1760.label: Top: in a passed-pawn endgame, moving/offering the bishop that blockaded the promotion square so the enemy KING grabs it (Kx) and the pawn queens; medium broadens to king-tempo and other piece/positional missteps that surrender control of a passed pawn (or its defended pawn), often without literally hanging a full piece.

1772.label: Top: a king move or back-rank defender's departure opens the first/last rank, allowing a forcing check that mates or wins material; medium broadens to general king walks into checks, forks, and mating nets (plus a few non-king-safety positional/tempo blurs).

1762.label: Top: a natural opening developing move (Bd3/Nf6/c6/Qf6) leaves the attacked central e-/d-pawn en prise instead of pushing it (e4/e5/d5); medium keeps the 'quiet move skips a forcing central break' signature but blurs toward materially-safe moves that merely miss a winning break/tactic rather than hang material.

1779.label: TOP: a knight is parked on an undefended square (often a 'outpost' sortie) and snapped off for free by a bishop (Bx-knight); MEDIUM keeps the hung knight but broadens the capturer to also include queen and knight.

1778.label: Top: a slow king move (Kb2/Ka3/Kd2) ignores an undefended knight, classically d4 under Nf5, dropping it free; medium broadens to other quiet moves (castling, bishop/pawn moves) that hang or deflect a defender of a piece, but mixes in several 0–4cp non-blunders.

1776.label: Top: dead-drawn endgames where a materially-safe king/bishop/pawn move mispositions the king and fails to stop the opponent's passed pawn (king too far, wrong opposition, abandoned blockade); medium blurs to a 'safe' king move that instead exposes the king to a decisive attack.

1767.label: Top: a queen move (a retreat/centralization, or a greedy capture like Qxe8) vacates a key defensive square next to the own king and is punished by forced mate or a crushing forcing attack (Qxg7#, Qc3+, etc.); medium keeps the queen-abandons-safety idea but blurs into greedy queen grabs (Qxf3/Qxb7/Qxh1) refuted by intermezzo checks for material, plus a few non-queen moves (Ka3, Bxh3, a5).

1763.label: Top boards are equal opening positions where a non-capturing developing move (skipping exd4/exd5) hangs the c4 bishop or e5 pawn; medium blurs to hanging pieces/pawns and allowing forks or mating attacks across all phases.

1771.label: At the peak a natural quiet/greedy move squanders a forced mate (#+3 to #+15); at medium it broadens to missing decisive material-winning tactics and longer mating nets, with the position staying winning either way.

1769.label: Top boards are self-weakening moves—queen abandoning a defender or king stepping into checks—punished by a forced mate (back-rank, smothered); medium blurs to passive or loose moves that concede material to forks, captures, and discovered attacks, plus a few missed wins.

1781.label: From a completely winning position the player loses their queen—at the peak almost always the queen itself, typically by capturing a defended pawn/piece (often with check) or promoting/moving it onto a square covered by a recapturer; at medium the pattern blurs to losing other major material (dropping the exchange/a rook, or trading queen for a knight) into a drawn or merely-better ending.

1780.label: At the peak it's overwhelmingly a knight fork delivering check that wins the enemy queen (Nf3+/Ne7+/Ng4+ etc.); at medium the target (winning the queen) stays constant but the tactic blurs to non-knight or non-checking shots (skewer Re4+, direct attack Bd4).

1774.label: At peak the player skips a forcing CHECK that wins a piece (rook check or knight fork like Rf7+/Nf4+/Rc4+) in an otherwise-won rook/king endgame, playing a quiet king or pawn move instead; at medium it blurs to broader missed precision—non-check double attacks (Bg6, Rf7+), forcing queen checks (Qd8+), tempo-losing king moves, and even some near-best/best moves—still revolving around squandered winning rook/queen endgames.

1783.label: Top boards are sharp passed-pawn promotion races blundered by a pawn push or losing rook move that flips a draw/win into a loss; medium broadens to passive king/rook moves that merely let a winning endgame advantage slip, mixing 'hangs' and 'missed' directions (plus several flagged non-blunders).

1773.label: Top boards relocate the sole defender (queen/rook/knight) off its post and drop material or the back rank to a forcing capture/check; medium broadens to the king itself walking into a forced mate and other defensive collapses that concede material or mate.

1794.label: Top: missed a forced checkmate (overwhelmingly mate-in-one, often caused by moving away the very piece sealing the mating net); medium: blurs to squandering an otherwise won position by an imprecise forcing move — wrong move-order, a slow/non-forcing move, or a check/capture that skips the decisive continuation (incl. longer forced mates).

1795.label: Top boards hang a piece via a premature opening knight foray (Nxe4/Nxf7/Ng4) refuted by the central ...d5 break or a queen grab; medium blurs to bishop retreats and tempo-losing moves that drop or fail to secure material.

1799.label: Top boards uniformly miss a single-ply capture of an undefended minor piece (mostly bishops, some knights) while sitting on a winning position; medium broadens to grabbing larger/other hanging pieces (rooks, knights) and to multi-move winning captures/tactics, with a couple of positional or own-material-hanging edge cases.

1793.label: Top: a premature pawn capture in the center releases tension and hands the opponent a dominating knight (occasionally bishop) outpost on the vacated square (d4/d5/e4/e5); medium keeps the same 'capture-releases-tension' error but broadens to flank/queenside captures (and even a push) that open files toward the king, create enemy passers, or allow a fork on the recapture square.

1792.chip: Hasty check hangs piece (or misses win)
1792.label: Top: a tempting forcing check (rook/queen/bishop) hangs the checking piece outright, often throwing away a forced mate; medium broadens to materially-safe checks that merely skip a stronger quiet/deflecting winning move.

1797.label: At the peak it's always a rook that captures a pawn (often with check) in a losing endgame and is immediately recaptured—a rook-for-pawn liquidation that throws away the last defensive piece; at medium it blurs to hanging other pieces (knight, queen) via greedy captures and even non-capture blunders like a king walking into mate or a skewer, in merely drawn/losing positions.

1788.label: Top boards are slow pawn/piece moves (b3, c4, bishop/knight retreats) that forfeit the one critical tempo — usually failing to kick a centralized enemy queen with c3/d5 — and bleed into lost material or a crushing attack; medium broadens to any passive move in a razor-thin one-move position that hangs material to varied tactics (back-rank, pins, trapped pieces, forks, king-attacks).

1802.label: Top boards are uniformly a missed h-pawn capture (hxg4, occasionally hxg5) of a hanging g-file minor piece that was pinning the f3-knight, with the player instead making a safe but non-capturing developing/pawn move in a won position; at medium it blurs into other missed material wins (Qxb4, Bxg7) and squandered winning positions via weakening pawn pushes or even self-hangs (Qc3, Nxf7), so the constant is 'declined a winning capture' while the specific hxg4-pin motif dissolves.

1808.label: Top is an unsound opening bishop sacrifice/check (Bxf2+) that drops the bishop for a pawn against an uncastled king; medium broadens to aggressive bishop checks (Bxe5+) refuted by a counterattacking fork, still losing the bishop/exchange — though several lower top boards drift into unrelated pawn/tempo losses.

1810.label: Top boards lose the queen by voluntarily moving it onto a capturable square — either hung outright or traded into a lost position; medium boards broaden to any move (developing, recapturing, opening a file/diagonal) that leaves the queen en prise or forces a losing queen trade.

1822.label: Top: an attacked minor piece (knight/bishop) is left directly en prise and grabbed for free next move; medium broadens to indirect hangs — removing the piece's sole defender, making a slow move while it dangles, or trading it for just a pawn (and occasionally a hung queen).

1806.label: Top: king moves (plus a couple pawn pushes) in already-lost pawn endgames that lose the king-and-pawn race, go the wrong direction, or walk into mate; medium blurs to rook/piece endgames and pawn pushes where the king is similarly mispositioned, pinned, exposed, or loses critical tempo.

1811.label: Top boards uniformly squander a winning position by playing a slow pawn push (or passive piece move) instead of a decisive rook penetration to the 2nd/7th rank; medium keeps the rook-invasion core but broadens to other missed winning shots (overloads, forks, captures) and to moves that actively hang material (back-rank mate, in-between captures, trapped knight).

1791.label: At the peak a quiet non-capturing pawn/king move leaves the opponent's hanging queen uncaptured, forfeiting a free queen (and usually the game to forced mate); at medium it broadens to skipping other winning tactics or playing king-safety/quiet moves that instead allow mate or drop the exchange/a pawn.

1824.label: Top positions are uniformly purposeless rook/queen checks in won-or-drawn endgames that lose a tempo and shove the enemy king to a BETTER square; medium blurs the trigger to any tempo-squandering or careless endgame move (passive king shuffles, blocking own passer, missing a forced mate, even a clean hang).

1818.label: Top: a non-defensive move (greedy capture or king shuffle) ignores a forcing refutation that mates or wins major material against the exposed king; medium keeps the same 'overlooked the threat' oversight but blurs the motif to assorted tactics (forks, skewers, back-rank mates, hung queens) and a few missed defensive resources/draws.

1845.label: Top: ignores a bishop already aiming at the queen along an open g5-d8 or g4-d1 diagonal, dropping it to Bxd8/Bxd1; medium broadens to self-inflicted exposure — opening the diagonal yourself (...e6) or moving the queen onto the bishop's line (Qd2, met by Bxd2+).

1803.label: Top: a quiet king/rook move (in a winning position) that hangs — or fails to capture — an exposed QUEEN amid mutual queen tension; medium blurs to hanging rooks/knights/pawns or walking into a mating attack.

1800.label: TOP: a quiet/non-forcing move (Rb8, O-O-O, b3, Nf3, Qe5) skips the thematic forcing bishop capture (Bxe3/Bxe6) and is refuted by a knight fork (Nxc7+/Nd6) or pin winning exchange/queen; MEDIUM broadens to any natural developing, retreating, or pawn-push move that ignores the tactical demand and is punished by varied captures, forks, or trapped pieces — mixing outright material loss with positional collapse.

1839.label: Top boards are all capture-trades of the last defensive minor piece (almost always a bishop) into a dead-lost king-and-pawn endgame; medium keeps the 'recapture-into-a-lost-position' core but blurs the piece/result — other trades (rook-for-knight, bishop swaps) into lost rook endings plus captures that simplify/open lines into outright tactics (forks, back-rank mate, enemy promotion).

1825.label: Top: a constructive-looking but non-forcing move (…d5, Na4-c5, …b4, …a6, Bd7) that ignores the position's concrete demands and drops material or invites a decisive break — peak cases hang a pawn/piece after a reposition or pawn push; medium narrows to the same kind of knight reroute (Nf3-e1) that abandons a defended pawn (a2) to a simple quiet capture.

1785.chip: Hangs piece via idle king move
1785.label: Top: king moves in drawn endgames that ignore a hanging enemy piece — the best move is a forcing capture (usually a free ROOK, sometimes a queen or knight) but the king wanders off, so the player drops or fails to win decisive material and goes from equal to lost; medium broadens away from king moves to other quiet moves (e.g., a pawn push) that lose material to a tactic such as a discovered check, and the direction blurs between hanging one's own piece and missing the free capture.

1830.label: At the peak the player plays a quiet developer and misses Bxg7 (or Bxb7/Bxg2 on the long diagonal), grabbing an undefended pawn to trap the h8/a8 rook and win the exchange; at medium it blurs to other missed material-winning tactics (Nc2+ fork, Qxb2/Qxc6 grabs, Qg6 attack) and bleeds into self-inflicted losses where opening a file/diagonal lets the opponent's rook or bishop win material.

1850.label: Top: an aggressive/forcing-looking move (illusory check or fork, capture, rook lift, pawn break) hangs a full piece or the exchange to an overlooked recapture/forcing sequence; medium broadens to the same self-refuting active move dropping only a pawn or squandering a winning advantage rather than a whole piece.

1857.label: Top boards are king moves (Kg4, Ka1, Rg1, Kg8) that step directly into a forced checkmate on an exposed king; medium broadens to any move (e.g. Rab8) that fails to flee the file/diagonal and leaves the king caught in a mating net — though a few top hits dilute into plain material/tempo losses rather than mate.

1841.label: Top: in a losing position the player plays a quiet/king move and misses capturing a hanging enemy queen (usually a free pawn capture like dxc5/exf6); medium broadens to passive king moves in already-lost positions that overlook the best defense and merely hasten the mate rather than grabbing a free piece.

1847.chip: Greedy capture exposes king (or hangs material)
1847.label: TOP: greedily grabbing a baited piece lets the opponent's queen/rook crash through for a decisive attack or mate on the player's OWN king; MEDIUM broadens to material-motivated moves that simply hang the piece, mis-order the capture, or skip a clean winning tactic.

1853.label: Top: a quiet/non-forcing move (pawn push, passive rook, routine capture) ignores a winning or game-saving forcing bishop check, very often Bd4+ on the long diagonal; medium: a check IS played but with the wrong piece (usually the queen) instead of the correct bishop/knight check, broadening from 'skipped the check entirely' to 'right idea, wrong piece/square.'

1856.chip: Hangs material in opening (often pawn push)
1856.label: Top = premature opening pawn advances (b4/c5/d5/e4) that hang a pawn or piece to a direct capture or one-move tactic; medium broadens to tempo-wasting 'question-the-bishop' pawn moves (h6/h3) and loose bishop captures (Bxf4/Bxh3/Ng5) that drop material to a refuting tactic.

1858.label: Top: a passive king move in a drawn/won pawn endgame that ignores the single critical pawn break (e5/c5/f5/g4), flipping the result by 500-700cp; Medium: broadens to general endgame tempo-loss — passive king retreats or premature pawn pushes instead of the right break/centralization (and a couple non-pawn cases), often only a few cp and mixing draw-to-loss with missed wins.

1855.label: Top: in a pure rook endgame a king/rook/queen move parks the piece on a rank or file shared with a friendly piece, hanging the rook (or queen) to a skewering/deflecting rook check; medium keeps the king-walks-into-trouble theme but broadens to any exposure tactic — knight forks, mate-in-one, trapped queen — plus minor positional/tempo lapses with varied material lost.

1863.label: At the peak it's a rook capture/exchange that liquidates a winning (or equal) ROOK-vs-minor position straight into a drawn or lost king-AND-PAWN endgame; medium blurs this to any piece exchange or recapture (rook-for-minor exchange sac, removing a key blockader, wrong pawn capture) that simplifies away the advantage into a worse endgame — note several top boards are actually correct liquidations, so the feature tracks the rook-into-pawn-endgame transition more than the blunder itself.

1859.label: Top: a passive queen retreat from the active central d5 post (Qd8/Qd7/Qe6/Qa5) that skips the only forcing reply (7...Bxf3 holding equality) and invites White's d5 push with tempo; medium broadens to other tempo-losing or purposeless piece moves (Bg4, Nc6, Qg8+, Bb2) that surrender the initiative or walk into tactics.

1854.label: Top: a rook (or other major piece) deserts a critical defensive square—often the back rank/key infiltration point—and is mated or loses a full piece to the enemy queen's capture; medium broadens to king and minor-piece moves that abandon defended pawns/squares or walk into checks and skewers, losing less material over one or two moves.

1837.label: Top boards are queen moves that permit a forced queen exchange liquidating a winning attack or forced mate (occasionally just hanging the queen to a pawn); medium broadens to hanging other pieces or conceding material that similarly dissolves the advantage.

1879.label: Top: ignores a knight on g6/g3 fronting a queen on h5/h4 and skips the saving hxg6/hxg3, allowing a discovered check that wins the rook or mates; medium broadens to hanging a piece or the exchange to any forcing refutation (overload, intermezzo, back-rank).

1881.chip: Hangs piece, often bishop to pawn
1881.label: Top boards uniformly hang a bishop to an enemy pawn capture in the opening (e.g. Bf4 ×exf4, Bf5 ×exf5, Bc5 ×dxc5); medium keeps the hung-piece theme but broadens to knight/queen/rook captured by various pieces and bleeds into looser tempo/positional opening errors.

1869.chip: Hangs pawn via overextended push (often e5)
1869.label: Top is a near-uniform undefended e4–e5 advance that simply hangs the pawn to ...Nxe5 (frequently also hitting the c4-bishop); medium blurs to other premature pawn pushes (b5, f5, g5, c5, e4) and a few piece moves that either drop a central pawn or, increasingly, just concede an outpost/king-safety rather than losing material outright.

1873.label: Top: in a clearly won position the player skips the decisive queen trade (Qxe3/Qxf6/Qxf7) that liquidates into a trivially won pawn/minor endgame, instead playing an aimless queen check or king move that lets the king escape into perpetual-check/draw range; medium broadens the same 'best move is Qx-trade declined' theme to non-winning cases — defensive/only-saving trades and outright leaving the queen hanging by ignoring its attack.

1860.label: Top: a quiet retreat or pawn-push fails to handle the e-file Rxe8+ Bxf6 Nxd5 motif (rook-trade, dark-bishop deflection of the f6/g7 cover, then a knight fork), losing material; medium: the same non-forcing 'tempo-loss' move blunders into broader forcing tactics — other knight forks (Nxc7+), simple piece/pawn wins (Nxe4, dxc4) or back-rank Rxe8+/Rxc1 — rather than the single e-file fork combination (note: several peak boards are the same motif seen from the attacker missing Rxe8+, blurring hung vs missed-win).

1864.label: Top boards are king moves in dead-drawn endgames that go to the edge, abandon a key square, or decline a drawing capture and collapse into forced mate; medium blurs to other piece moves (rook/knight) and to already-lost positions with only minor eval swings, mixed with several non-blunder king moves.

1884.label: Top boards drop a full bishop in the opening for free—usually by moving instead of capturing an en-prise intruder (Bf3/Bf6) or planting the bishop on an undefended square; medium broadens to knights, queen, and pieces lost over 2-3 move tactical refutations (forks, discovered attacks, trapped pieces) but the constant remains a one-move material giveaway in the opening.

1885.label: Top: a rook exchange (usually via a check, e.g. Rg5+/Rb3+/Re2+) that liquidates into a king-and-pawn ending the player has misjudged as holdable but is lost; medium broadens to queen trades into pawn endings and, more loosely, other favorable liquidations/captures (hung pawn or exchange, wrong-order checks).

1886.label: Top boards hang a piece (often a bishop) by moving its sole defender or walking into a capture, punished by a 1–3 move tactic; medium broadens to hanging the queen (knight forks / undefended on an open file), allowing outright mate, plus a few cases of a safe move skipping a winning exchange-sac/capture.

1871.label: Top: a slow or wrong-pawn move forfeits a passed-pawn promotion race so the opponent queens first or the king is cut off; medium blurs into any tempo-wasting/passive move that surrenders the initiative, the win, or allows a tactic.

1872.label: Top: a relocating king/queen/knight/rook abandons the sole defender of a piece (rook f1, rook d8, queen, bishop) or its own king, losing a major piece or allowing forced mate; medium broadens to king moves that merely walk into checks/exposed squares for smaller or already-lost losses (and one passive tempo move missing a win).

1888.chip: Hangs piece on aggressive sortie (often knight)
1888.label: Top: a knight (occasionally bishop) thrust to an aggressive advanced square (h4/e5/g4/d4/g5/h5) is left undefended/trapped and snapped off for free; medium broadens to bishops, queens and pawn pushes that hang the moved unit or vacate a defender, still losing material.

1889.label: Top: rook checks in won K+R endgames that hand the king a tempo and delay the forced mate; medium broadens to queen checks and bigger swings that outright forfeit a forced mate (mate-in-4/6) instead of playing the quiet improving move.

1896.chip: Hangs to a check (often f7/f2 queen)
1896.label: Top: a developing/quiet move ignores the queen battery and drops the f2/f7 pawn to a queen capture WITH CHECK that wrecks king safety; medium keeps the 'lose material to a forcing check' core but broadens the check type and target square (Qxb2+/Qxd4+ after a defender leaves, Qd1+ back-rank, discovered e5+, Greek-gift Bxh7+, Rxa7+).

1893.label: Top positions uniformly skip the winning central pawn break (almost always ...d5/d4, frequently winning the c4-bishop or punishing a misplaced queen) in favor of a slow developing/queen/castling move; medium keeps the 'played a quiet move, missed the forcing win' core but the missed shot broadens from the central break to other tactics (forks, discovered attacks, e5/c4 levers).

1891.label: Top: unsound rook/bishop sacrifices thrown at the enemy king (g/h-file) that a simple recapture refutes, squandering a winning position; medium broadens to any material-losing capture—hanging a minor piece, recapturing/capturing with the wrong piece, or liquidating a dominant piece in a bad trade.

1902.chip: Tempo loss in won position (piece chased)
1902.label: At the peak, negligible tempo-losing king/pawn moves in totally won endgames (Kg2, h5 ~9-12cp); at medium it broadens to placing a piece on a harassable square (Bg4) where it gets chased and eventually concedes a pawn/tempo.

1899.label: Top: a king move (often grabbing a pawn) walks the king onto an exposed square, allowing a forced mate or perpetual via consecutive checks; medium broadens to king/defender moves that expose the king to checks and forks winning material rather than mate, with a few pure piece-hangs (fork, hanging piece, back rank) mixed in.

1906.label: Top boards are all winning positions where the player skipped a forcing fork or direct capture that wins the opponent's QUEEN, instead playing a slow/wrong-move-order move that lets the queen escape; medium broadens the 'decisive thing missed' to also include forced mates and wrong-order captures that squander an already-winning advantage.

1892.label: Top: drawn king-and-pawn/promotion endgames where a king or bishop misplacement fails to control the queening square or win the pawn race (letting the opponent promote), with a couple of cases of a knight missing the only saving queen-capture; medium broadens to any wrong-direction or tempo-losing king/piece move that throws away a holdable endgame.

1910.label: Top is laser-focused: Black recaptures the c6-knight with bxc6 while uncastled, hanging the exchange to the Bxc6+ check-fork of king and a8-rook; medium blurs this into assorted opening moves that hang material to a tactic (other forks, pins, hanging pieces), not just the bxc6/Bxc6+ motif.

1908.label: Top is uniformly the player's own sacrificial/forcing check (esp. knight checks Nf3+/Ne7+/Nf6+, plus Bxf7+/Rf8+) that simply hangs the piece to a recapture or counter-check; medium blurs to quiet captures and pawn moves refuted by the opponent's intermezzo check or fork, with a few missed-win checks mixed in.

1913.label: Top boards are uniform: a knight delivered as a fork-CHECK that simply gets captured (rook/knight takes the undefended knight) -> hangs knight; medium blurs to other tempting forcing checks (queen, rook, even O-O) that either lose material or, increasingly, skip a stronger win/mate, so the constant is 'flashy check that backfires' while the material-loss specificity (hangs knight) weakens at medium toward missed-win/positional errors.

1909.label: Top: a king-exposing move (pawn-shield push, king march, or diverted defender) that permits a forced mate/decisive attack on one's own king; medium broadens to general material blunders—hung pieces, undefended-piece forks, and tempo-losing retreats.

1901.label: Top: while already winning, the player skips a free capture of an undefended enemy piece (often the queen, mostly a major piece), playing a safe non-capture and squandering a forced mate; medium blurs by also covering leaving one's OWN major piece en prise (mutual-hanging situations, premature promotion) and missing faster non-capturing forced mates.

1823.label: Top: a piece is relocated off its key defensive square/tactical resource (Rd1, Nf6+, d-file), squandering a near-won position and often hanging material; medium keeps the 'abandons defensive duty' core but broadens to greedy pawn-grabs and king-safety blunders that desert defense and concede the edge.

1903.label: Top: knight fork-checks (Nc7+/Nf7) hang because the target square is guarded so the queen/king recaptures (clean piece loss); medium broadens to wrong-piece or move-order checks (Qh4+, Ba3+, Rd8+) that let the king escape and squander a forced win rather than losing material.

1904.label: Top: opening positions where the player hangs a piece by ignoring a capture threat in the center (often skipping the trivial Qxd4/Qxd5 capture/recapture and leaving an own central knight/pawn en prise); medium blurs into general tactical oversights — also missing free captures/forks and allowing the opponent's tactic (king-safety/defender-removal) — and drifts into the middlegame, mixing hung-own with missed-win.

1925.label: At the peak, a quiet developing/king-safety move (Ndf3, O-O, Bh2, a3) squanders the winning Nxf7! knight sacrifice against an uncastled king; at medium it broadens to skipping any forcing tactical win (deflection captures like Nxc3/Nxc6, forks like Nxf2, tempo shots like Bc4+) from an already-winning position.

1911.label: Top boards are king-exposing or defender-abandoning moves that walk into a decisive forcing check delivering mate or winning the queen by king-fork; medium keeps the 'abandon a defended square' gesture but blurs the target to general forks and material loss (piece/pawn) not necessarily on the king.

1915.label: Top: needless opening king moves (Ke2/Kf2/Kd2/Ke7) that forfeit castling and expose the king, usually conceding a free central pawn; Medium: broadens to king-exposing moves in any phase—walking into Qa4+/Qxg7+ checks, mating nets, or O-O-O into an attack—plus a few non-king king-safety lapses.

1919.label: Top: a voluntary king move steps onto an exposed square and walks straight into a check or knight fork that wins material (Nf4+, Nd5+, Nc4, Qh3+); medium keeps the same exposed-king-move motif but broadens the punishment to discovered checks/attacks (Nxc8+, d7+), king-hunts toward mate, and a few mistimed king moves that hang or miss in passed-pawn/promotion settings.

1924.chip: Faulty king move drops material (also rook/knight)
1924.label: Top: a king move (91%) that abandons a defended pawn/piece, loses critical tempo, or walks into a mating net; medium blurs to rook/knight repositioning that is too slow or hangs material, frequently letting the enemy rook seize the 7th/back rank.

1926.label: Top: a voluntary queen trade/move punished by a rook recapture (hanging the queen or stamping a rook on the 7th); medium blurs to other moves that concede material or a decisive breakthrough/fork/mate without the queen-vs-rook signature.

1929.label: Top: own minor piece (usually a bishop) moves into an enemy knight's capture range; medium blurs to rooks/exchange left undefended and king/castling moves, but all drop material to an immediate knight capture.

1923.label: Top: a passed pawn is shoved one square toward promotion (7th/2nd rank) and the enemy KING steps in front to blockade and win the pawn over 2-3 moves, where 'king-first' activation was the win; medium broadens to other tempo-wasting endgame moves (king/rook repositionings, plus pushes) that let the passer be blockaded or outraced, with several borderline (0-cp) cases mixed in.

1930.label: Top: moving the pinned f3-knight (Ne5) unmasks the d1-queen and hangs it to Bxd1 in the opening; medium broadens to hanging any piece (queen, rook, exchange) by vacating its guard/blocker or ignoring an enemy tactic (incl. forks/mates).

1917.label: Top boards are near-identical: a routine opening developer that skips the winning Nb5→Nc7+ (or Nb4→Nxc2+) knight fork of king and rook; medium blurs the fork motif into broader opening tactical lapses — other missed wins, hung pieces from unsound sacs, and structural/king-safety errors.

1935.label: Top: a materially-safe endgame king/knight move ignores a free enemy-QUEEN capture that was the only good move (Rxb8/Nxh5/Nxb6); medium: the same passive king move skips a lower-value saving resource — capturing a knight, capturing a pawn to stop promotion, or trading to avoid back-rank mate.

1932.label: Top: a move — usually the king itself (king 65%) — walks onto an open file/diagonal or strips the king's last guard, allowing a forcing check sequence that ends in forced mate; medium keeps the same king-exposure mechanism but broadens to moving away a defender (rook/bishop) or weakening the back rank, where the refuting checks win decisive material rather than always delivering immediate mate.

1918.label: Top: a quiet/structural move drops own material outright (rook→queen→knight→exchange) by deserting a defender or opening a line; medium broadens to slow moves that instead squander a winning forcing tactic (missing the win), with only some still hanging material.

1946.label: Top boards uniformly leave the queen en prise to an enemy bishop along an open/just-opened diagonal (Bxd8/Bxh3/Bxc3); medium keeps the hung queen but the capturer occasionally becomes a knight and lines open more via removed shields.

1942.label: Top: a quiet/greedy move skips a queen check (often an intermediate check exploiting the exposed king) that wins a rook; medium broadens to any missed forcing winner—knight forks, mate sequences, or other pieces—occasionally even a chosen check that hangs material.

1939.label: Top: in an already-losing endgame, a bishop (sometimes knight) captures the enemy rook and is recaptured, liquidating into a lost king-and-pawn endgame; medium broadens to rook-for-rook trades and even non-capturing tempo-losing king moves that still concede the lost pawn endgame.

1948.label: Top boards are losing rook/pawn endgames where a defensive rook move allows a rook trade transposing into a hopelessly lost king-and-pawn endgame (Rxg8/Rxc1/Rxh4/Rxf3) — or leaves the rook passive/walks into mate; medium blurs the 'rook-trade' constant into any material-losing endgame/middlegame blunder: hanging a piece (Nf6+→Nxf6), allowing a fork, walking into mate (Rad8→Qf7#, a5→Bh5), missing a perpetual, or pointless checks across pieces and phases.

1938.label: Top boards consistently punish a move-order/priority error around a passed pawn — capturing or developing/defending instead of pushing the passer with tempo (or correct sequencing) to keep a winning advantage; medium blurs to any wrong-priority/wrong-plan move that throws away a forcing win (promotion race, forced mate, or tactical shot), and includes some outright hangs and a couple of false positives.

1949.label: Top: in a won passed-pawn endgame, advanced the pawn instead of capturing the knight/bishop that blockades or defends the promotion square (e.g. Kxh2/Kxg7/bxa5), letting a blockade form and squandering the win; medium broadens to general tempo-wasting moves in won pawn endings — pushing the wrong passer, king shuffles, impulsive checks, even abandoning a defender — and includes a couple of non-blunders, so the precise 'kill the blockader' core blurs into 'fail to make the one converting move.'

1912.label: Top: a slow, quiet move in a winning position skips a decisive fork/double-attack (best move forks two pieces), often also hanging a piece; medium broadens to general tactical blunders — hanging pieces or the queen and allowing forced mate — in noisier, sometimes-losing positions.

1931.label: At the peak the player overlooks a clean, winning capture of an undefended enemy piece — almost always a ROOK — typically playing a king move or pointless check instead (and several leak that same material via a 1-3 move refutation, e.g. Kb3→Rxc3+); at medium it blurs to any piece (queen/knight/bishop) and to adjacent material decisions: missed recaptures, missed promotion/tactic, hanging one's own queen, or allowing mate, so the direction splits between 'missed a free capture' and 'hung own piece.'

1953.label: Top: an inferior queen check in a drawn/winning endgame lets the king escape and squanders the result (the precise alternative was a different check that wins material); medium broadens to milder near-zero inaccuracies and non-check rook/queen repositioning moves in similar endgames.

1956.label: Top: in a balanced opening a quiet pawn/developing move (esp. 5.d3) leaves the Italian Bc4 en prise to ...dxc4, dropping the bishop; medium broadens the same 'ignored a pawn-capture threat / central tension' motif to hanging other minors (f4-bishop, c6/f6-knights) or even the queen, with a couple of tempo-loss cases that concede material over a few moves.

1961.label: Top: a king move in a drawn/lost endgame that burns a tempo or abandons a key square (too far from the pawn race, goes passive, releases the enemy king); medium keeps the endgame tempo/wrong-plan theme but blurs the moving piece — pawn pushes, bishop/knight relocations, even king walks the wrong way — and bleeds into a few moves that simply hasten the loss or allow a mating attack.

1965.label: Top: a piece relocated/retreated to a passive square (very often the Nimzo b4-bishop) abandons its pressure/defensive role and gets trapped or lost to a pawn break; medium blurs to any piece hung through wrong-order captures, direct undefended moves, or even tempo/finesse errors that squander a win.

1927.label: Top: every board plays a routine developing/castling/repositioning move and misses the SAME central pawn thrust (d4/e4/d5/e5) that forks White's knight AND bishop in the opening; Medium: still mostly a quiet move squandering a winning resource, but the specific motif blurs — a couple stay pure pawn forks (d5, f5+ on king+rook), while the rest broaden to other missed tactics (Bb5, Bxe7) or greedy captures that hang material (gxh5, Qd7).

1952.label: Top: queen moves/checks (Qe8+, Qxe7+, Qxg5+) that throw away a completely won endgame into a draw or loss; medium blurs to pawn-endgame pushes squandering the win, with several near-zero-loss non-blunders mixed in.

1950.label: Top boards almost uniformly hinge on the Nd5/Nd4 central knight leap that attacks the enemy queen on the f-file in sharp open games (a slow/tempo-losing move misses it as White's Nd5 or Black's Nd4, or directly allows the opponent's Nd5/recapture); medium broadens to other knight leaps that attack the queen or fork material (Ne3, Ng4, Nd3, Ne4+) and slides toward outright hung/greedy pawn grabs, so the constant peak motif is the d5/d4 knight-vs-queen strike while the destination square and exact direction blur at medium.

1968.label: Top: a pawn-endgame king move that surrenders the opposition (or the key central square), letting the enemy king march in and pick off pawns; medium broadens to general endgame king mispositioning/tempo-loss (wrong direction, passive retreat, abandoning a guard square) with a few non-king positional/tactical errors mixed in.

1955.label: Top: queen left en prise to a bishop sweeping an open long diagonal (g4/g5), captured outright next move; medium keeps the hung-queen-to-diagonal-bishop core but blurs to hanging knights/the exchange and a few materially-safe queen trades that just throw away a winning advantage.

1972.label: Top: moving the e4 knight off the e-file (Nf6/Ng5/Nxd2/Nxf2) unleashes a Nc6+ discovered check that wins Black's queen in the Petrov opening; medium keeps the 'piece move opens a line for a discovered check winning material' idea but blurs to other files/squares (Be5+, Nf5+, Nxf3+) and mixes in unrelated material-losing oversights (hung pieces, tempo, sac).

1970.label: Top boards almost all walk a king/knight into a discovered check that wins the queen (esp. the Petrov ...Nf6→Nxc6+ trap); medium broadens the loss from queen to piece/exchange and bleeds into adjacent king-exposure tactics (back-rank mate, fork, promotion).

1978.label: Top: an opening move develops/advances one piece while leaving another sitting cleanly en prise for an immediate free capture (queen most dramatic, but also bishop/knight/pawn); medium blurs the mechanism, broadening to material lost over a few moves via short tactics — forks, trapped bishop, unsound sacrifices and king-side weakening (plus one odd missed-mate).

1981.label: Top: a king-flight (sometimes queen) 'safety' move that skips the only forced defensive capture/queen-trade and walks straight into forced mate; medium keeps the 'ignored the urgent threat instead of the forced defense' core but broadens the move type (queen sorties, greedy captures, pawn pushes) and the punishment (material loss as well as mate).

1958.label: Top: voluntarily liquidates the key defensive knight/bishop via a capture/exchange that recaptures into a clearly LOST king-and-pawn endgame; medium broadens to losing a minor piece more generally — outright hanging it (king/defender steps away, undefended check) or sacrificing it for a losing position, including non-endgame blunders.

1984.chip: Hangs queen to bishop pin (king-line tactics)
1984.label: Top is near-uniform: queen left on the a7–g1 diagonal with the king on g1 and lost to ...Bc5 pin (Kh1 was the cure; #7/#10 are the rook- and e8-king variants); medium blurs into general king/queen line-exposure — bishop/queen forks (Bb3, Qe5+, Qd3+) and kings walking into checks/skewers on open files/diagonals.

1969.label: Top boards almost all skip grabbing a hanging enemy major piece—usually the queen—by playing a check or king move instead; medium broadens to overlooking minor-piece captures, plus hanging one's own piece or walking into mate.

1975.label: Top: in a won position a careless or wrong-order move lets the opponent force perpetual check, drawing the game (king-safety lapses); medium broadens to squandering the winning advantage via any counterplay—king checks, mating attacks, or even hanging material / missing a free capture.

1987.label: Top: in a lost endgame the player abandons the blockade/promotion-control square and the opponent's passed pawn queens (often with check); medium blurs into general lost-position blunders—walking the king into mate and other material-losing moves.

1990.label: Top boards are rook-for-rook trades on an open file/back rank that surrender the file, ditch a key defender, or skip a stronger tactic; medium broadens to premature trades and captures generally—queen swaps, rook sacrifices, wrong-order captures, and grabbing material over a forced win.

1985.label: Top boards are won positions where the player skips the single decisive rook trade/sacrifice that liquidates into a winning pawn endgame (Rxf2+, Rxc7+, Rxe3+...), keeping the rook active instead; medium broadens to any missed winning capture/tactic at the critical moment (Bxf1, Bxe3+, Qxd1+), with a minority instead hanging a piece (queen/bishop/rook).

1991.chip: Hangs pawn ignoring central tension (medium piece)
1991.label: Top: a quiet developing/prophylactic opening move skips the timely central capture (fxe5/cxd5/exd5/dxe5) and drops a central pawn; medium keeps the central-tension theme but broadens to hanging full pieces and to merely missing winning central captures.

1982.label: Top boards consistently waste a critical tempo or strip the lone defender and let an enemy passed pawn promote; medium keeps the 'neglected urgent threat' shape but broadens to forks, mating attacks, hanging defenders, and even a missed winning tactic.

1989.label: Top: in an already-lost endgame the player promotes/pushes a pawn or moves the king the wrong way without king support, hanging the new queen or abandoning the passer; medium blurs into king moves walking into mating nets plus assorted pawn-push/knight blunders that hang material or lose tempo while losing.

1994.label: Top boards nearly all miss the winning Nxf7 (Fried-Liver f7-sacrifice from a g5-knight + Bc4 battery), retreating/repositioning instead; medium keeps the 'winning position, declined forcing shot' core but blurs to other missed tactics — knight forks (Na4, Nd2), other sacrifices (Nxh7, Nxf8, Bxf7+) and double attacks — with the f7 motif still recurring.

1996.label: Top boards are early queen sorties (Qa5/Qh5/Qe7/Qa4) to exposed squares that get trapped on h1 or hit with a tempo-gaining develop-and-attack (Bd2/Bb5+/Bd7), dropping the queen or material; medium keeps the 'move walks into a refutation that costs material' core but blurs to any piece walking into a fork, pin, or trap (and a few missed-tactic cases).

1986.label: Top boards consistently play a check or idle move while leaving an enemy passed pawn one step from queening when the only move was to capture/block it (classic 'sees a check'); medium boards blur to any tempo-wasting, inaccurate move that squanders the single correct resource at a critical moment—allowing a fork, missing king centralization or prophylaxis, or frittering away a won endgame.

1998.label: Top: an opening bishop developed/left on an undefended, directly-attacked square is captured for free (Bb5/Bf5/Bg4/Bg5, or a bishop on b4 abandoned by a knight move); medium keeps the same hung-bishop-in-the-opening core but blurs into indirect hangs (moving another piece while a g5-bishop is en prise), the occasional knight drop, and related trade/positional material losses.

2001.label: Top boards consistently leave a bishop en prise after an unrelated/king move (often capturable by the enemy king or via a pin), while medium positions broaden to hanging knights, rooks and queens and blur into greedy pawn-grabs and abandoned-defender oversights.

2013.label: Top: played a quiet/greedy move and missed a forcing QUEEN-CHECK sequence exploiting the exposed enemy king to win material or mate (Qd5+/Qe4+/Qh5+/Qf3+/Qg4+); medium broadens to other forcing king-hunts — knight/bishop checks, mating nets, forks and move-order wins — still against an exposed king.

2000.label: Top boards hang a BISHOP onto a square where a forcing capture/tactic (decoy, recapture-with-check, removed king-defender) wins it or mates; medium broadens to hung knights/pawns and blurs into tempo/positional eval drops where the loose piece or thrown-away tempo simply loses material.

2011.label: Top: a greedy capture (king/knight grabbing a bishop or the wrong pawn) in a K+P endgame wastes the one tempo needed to halt an enemy passed pawn, which then queens by force; medium blurs the capture requirement to any quiet tempo-wasting or wrong-square move that loses the pawn race or lets the king infiltrate, plus a few non-pawn tactical/king-safety outliers.

2019.label: Top: a quiet developing move (usually a bishop placement, sometimes castling/knight) leaves two minor pieces aligned so a pawn thrust (e4/e5/d4/c5) forks and wins one; medium keeps the pawn-fork motif but broadens the targets (king+rook via e4+, Be6/Nc6 via d5, Bg2/Ne2 via f3) and blurs into related trapped-piece/missed-shot losses.

1977.label: Top boards consistently overlook the strongest capture/intermezzo winning (or saving) the QUEEN, instead playing a lesser capture, check, or quiet move; medium broadens the forfeited-or-lost material to rooks, the exchange, and minor pieces, and the direction blurs between missing a win and hanging own material.

2005.label: Top: in a won endgame the player queens a pawn immediately instead of the required preparatory move (securing a pawn, stopping the enemy counter-promotion, removing an active piece, or sidestepping a skewer/mate), squandering or outright blundering the win; medium: the same move-order/prophylaxis failure blurs into other natural endgame moves (rook or king) that lose a tempo or abandon a key file/square, handing the opponent the one saving counterplay resource.

2002.label: Top: a (usually bishop) capture—Bxe2/Bxd2/Bxf3/Bxd7—that gets recaptured into a forced queen exchange and dissolves a winning/equal advantage instead of keeping the pin or tension; medium broadens to other premature releasing captures, wrong-piece grabs, and tempo-losing moves that squander a won position.

1993.label: Top: ignores a free en-prise enemy piece—usually the queen, sometimes a rook—and instead plays a quiet king/piece/pawn move that hangs its own material (or skips the win); medium blurs into natural-looking moves (greedy pawn grab, passive rook, knight retreat) that lose material or positional ground more subtly.

2024.label: Top boards waste a tempo with a pointless rook check before promoting (the cleaner immediate queen/promotion path); medium boards broaden to capturing a piece or pawn first—or underpromoting—instead of the immediate winning promotion.

2027.label: Top: passed up grabbing an undefended corner rook (Bxh8/Bxa8/Qxa1) on the wide-open long diagonal created by a fianchetto gap; medium keeps the 'skipped a free win' theme but broadens the target to any hanging piece/pawn (knight on c6/a3, g7/g2 pawn, also a Qxa8 rook), plus an occasional trapped-piece tactic.

2007.chip: Let enemy passed pawn promote (rook endgame)
2007.label: Top: in rook (or king-and-pawn) endgames the player abandons control of an enemy passed pawn—grabbing a side pawn or shuffling instead of blockading—so the passer queens and usually wins the rook within 2-3 moves; medium broadens beyond the constant passed-pawn theme to other pieces deserting their defensive task (queen failing to blockade, king/knight losing coordination) and to general material concessions from quiet, non-recapturing endgame moves.

2022.label: Top boards hang a pawn/piece with a premature central pawn push, overwhelmingly ...d5 met by cxd5 with no clean recapture (knight on c6 can't cover d5); medium broadens to other central breaks (...e5, d4/d5, e4) and occasional piece moves that lose material through captures, forks, opened diagonals, or trapped pieces.

2021.label: Top: a king move or threat-ignoring capture exposes the king and walks straight into a forced checkmate; medium: the same self-endangering, threat-ignoring move blurs to losing material generally (queen/piece forks, hanging pieces, even tempo/positional slips) rather than a clean forced mate.

2018.label: At the peak the move is a greedy/automatic capture (recapture, capture-with-check, or trade of a key defensive piece) that overlooks a forcing refutation and drops material or walks into mate; at medium it broadens to quiet king walks, pawn pushes, and queen retreats that abandon a key defender and allow the same decisive tactic.

2031.label: Top boards are uniformly a bishop left en prise to a rook capture, typically in an endgame after a non-defending pawn push or king move; medium boards keep the 'undefended piece grabbed (usually by a rook)' core but broaden the hung piece to queens, rooks and knights, plus a few greedy pawn-grabs that abandon a piece.

2023.label: Top boards are uniform: in a lost endgame the player pushes a pawn onto a guarded square and the freshly-promoted queen is captured for free; medium blurs the promotion specificity, keeping only the broader pattern of hanging material (piece, exchange, or losing the promotion/blockade race) while already lost in the endgame.

2012.label: Top boards all decline Bxe6+/Bc4+ — a light-squared bishop check on the a2-g8 diagonal against a king on g8 — for a quiet or retreating move; medium keeps the 'only one forcing move was good' skeleton but broadens to other light-square sacs/checks (Greek-gift Bxh7+, Bh5+, Qxe6+) with some drift into positional/king-safety errors.

2030.label: Top boards are uniformly a rook moved into (or left in) a knight's capture square (Nxrook), while medium broadens both axes — any piece (queen/bishop/rook) hung to any capturer (knight/bishop/pawn), with a few cases shading into plain tempo loss.

2043.label: Top: in a won middlegame, plays a quiet rook/king move and misses a forcing knight check that forks/wins material (Nf6+, Nf3+, Ne7+, often a sacrifice exploiting back-rank or e-file alignment); medium broadens to other knight tactics like exchange-winning Nxf6+ and back-rank Nd3, the same one-tempo-too-slow missed win.

2037.label: Top: a quiet/passive (usually pawn) move in an already-worse position ignores a forced rook-exchange sequence down an open file (consistently the e-file) that wins via a decisive passed c-pawn; medium keeps the 'ignored forcing rook-trade' core but blurs the decisive resource to other files, back-rank mates and endgame conversions—and mixes in missed wins as well as hung material.

2033.label: Top: a routine developing move hangs the QUEEN to an opening tactic (f3-knight pin →Bxf3, or Bg5/Bb5 →Bxd8/Bxd7+); medium broadens to hanging other material (piece, exchange, pawn, even mate) and frequently flips to MISSING a winning tactic (e5/e4, Qh4+, ...g5 trap) instead.

2028.label: Top: a rook delivers a capturing check (Rxd8+, Rxe8+, Rxe7+, Re1+, Rf2+) that the queen simply recaptures with the king safe, dropping the exchange or a full rook; medium blurs this into rook checks that merely trade into a lost game (Rc8+) and even off-pattern non-checking moves that lose material to a simple refutation.

2039.label: Top: greedily capturing the queen (usually Bxd1 with the bishop) while overlooking the Bxf7+ sac that delivers mate/fork; medium broadens to other greedy/natural moves that miss the tactical refutation — pawn grabs chased by tempo, hung pieces, and f7 forks — so 'queen→Bxf7 mate' at the peak blurs into 'any material grab punished by a tactic'.

2044.label: Top: a rook move onto a file/square shared with (or exposed to) the enemy rook lets a tempo-gaining knight check—fork or discovered attack (Nf6+/Nf8+/Nf4+/Nd6+/Ng6+)—deflect the king and win the rook; medium blurs to looser piece moves punished by varied deflecting checks, traps, and some missed wins/tempo-losses.

2025.label: Top boards almost uniformly lose material—usually the queen itself—by skipping the available queen trade (Qxd8/Qxd1) on the open d-file, leaving the king/queen exposed to a winning capture or fork; medium broadens to hanging the queen on various open lines via other move-order errors and even unsound queen sacrifices, plus a few non-queen tempo/premature-capture blunders.

2045.label: Top: in a winning position, played a passive pawn/king move or greedy capture instead of a forcing queen check (clinching a mate, queen-trade-to-won-endgame, or initiative), often letting in perpetual; medium broadens the missed forcing move to rook/bishop checks, capture-checks, mate-in-ones, and even a drawing check, with a couple blurring into outright hangs.

2020.label: Top: in a clearly winning opening, a quiet developing pawn/bishop move leaves a whole piece (most strikingly the queen) hanging to a simple capture; medium keeps the same 'winning position squandered by a quiet move' shape but blurs to pawn pushes/exchanges that merely bleed the advantage (lose a pawn, open lines) rather than dropping a full piece.

2046.label: Top boards are uniformly endgame moves that leave the player's own rook hanging to a winning check (skewer, deflection, back-rank/file pin); medium keeps the endgame forcing-check theme but blurs in direction and scope, mostly MISSING decisive checks/tactics (skewer, mate-in-N, promotion save) or walking into mate/fork.

2047.label: Top is constant: a natural or greedy capture skips a forced mate or queen-winning attack on the exposed enemy king (often back-rank); at medium the direction blurs, the move instead hanging a piece or allowing a tactic against the player's own king.

2041.label: Top: in a drawn/losing pawn endgame the player pushes their own passed pawn (h4/f4/g4/g3) or burns a tempo instead of capturing/stopping the opponent's already-advanced passer, which then queens; medium broadens to subtler king-placement and tempo errors in passed-pawn endgames that let the enemy pawn promote or (in a couple cases) throw away a win to a blockade/perpetual.
